paragraphs.text: Eruvin 2a–2b: ‘We find that the Mishkan is called Mikdash, and that the Mikdash is called Mishkan. For if you do not say so, consider Rav Yehudah’s statement in Shmuel’s name: Peace offerings slaughtered before the doors of the Heichal are opened are invalid, for it says, “He shall slaughter it at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting”—when it is open, and not when it is locked. Yet that verse was written concerning the Mishkan! Rather, we find that the Mikdash is called Mishkan and the Mishkan is called Mikdash. That the Mikdash is called Mishkan is clear, for it is written, “I shall place My Mishkan among you.” But from where do we learn that the Mishkan is called Mikdash? … From this verse: “They shall make Me a Mikdash, and I shall dwell among them.”’

paragraphs.text: Chavos Yair 210: ‘One should direct his intention only to the Cause of every cause, the Creator of heaven and earth.… A new prayer book was recently printed by a scholar established in Torah and fear of God.… One of the ordinary householders asked me to explain the author’s instruction to say, before putting on tefillin and tzitzis, and in several other places, “For the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence, through that which is hidden and concealed.” I answered that these words were intended only for outstanding Torah scholars. He replied that he was not asking to say it or to understand its subject, but only that I tell him the meaning of the words.… To appease him, I told him to believe me on my word of honor that I too do not understand the ultimate meaning and import of these words; and this is indeed the truth.’

paragraphs.text: Berachos 35b: ‘Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa said: Whoever enjoys this world without a blessing is as though he robs the Holy One, blessed be He, and the congregation of Israel, as it says, “One who robs his father and his mother and says, ‘There is no transgression,’ is a companion to a destructive man.” “His father” means none other than the Holy One, blessed be He, as it says, “Is He not your Father, who acquired you?” “His mother” means none other than the congregation of Israel, as it says, “Hear, my son, your father’s instruction, and do not forsake your mother’s Torah.”’

paragraphs.text: Megillah 29a: ‘Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai teaches: Come and see how beloved Israel is before the Holy One, blessed be He: wherever they were exiled, the Divine Presence was with them. They were exiled to Egypt, and the Divine Presence was with them, as it says, “Did I not reveal Myself to your father’s house when they were in Egypt?” They were exiled to Babylonia, and the Divine Presence was with them, as it says, “For your sake I was sent to Babylonia.” Even when they are destined to be redeemed, the Divine Presence will be with them, as it says, “The Lord your God will return with your captivity.” It does not say “He will bring back,” but “He will return”: this teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, returns with them from among the exiles.’

paragraphs.text: Bamidbar Rabbah 9:7: ‘I said, “For the Lord’s portion is His people; Jacob is the cord of His inheritance.” I took Jacob as an inheritance, and he was My portion, because his offspring resembled a cord whose strands are linked to one another: they were all of established lineage, the children of their fathers, with no other offspring interrupting them. They all guarded themselves against adultery, and there was no illegitimate lineage among them. How so? It is written, “Elazar begot Pinchas; Pinchas begot Avishua,” and so with them all: the chain continued in this manner.’

paragraphs.text: Berachos 32a: ‘“Because of the inability of the Lord”—should it not have said, “Because the Lord could not”? Rabbi Elazar said: Moses said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the world, now the nations of the world will say that His strength has grown weak like a female’s, and that He cannot save. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: Have they not already seen the miracles and mighty deeds I performed for them at the sea? He replied: Master of the world, they can still say that He could withstand one king, but could not withstand thirty-one kings. Rabbi Yochanan said: From where do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, ultimately agreed with Moses? For it says, “The Lord said, ‘I have forgiven according to your words.’”’

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 30b: A baraita teaches that Rabbi says: ‘It is revealed and known to the One who spoke and the world came into being that a son honors his mother more than his father, because she persuades him with words. God therefore placed honoring one’s father before honoring one’s mother. It is likewise revealed and known to Him that a son fears his father more than his mother, because his father teaches him Torah. God therefore placed reverence for one’s mother before reverence for one’s father.’

paragraphs.text: Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 10, 25b: ‘Yod and heh are fear and love, Father and Mother, the right arm and the left arm, kindness and might.… Vav is Torah, which rests in the mouth; through the breath of the mouth it flies upon the eagle.… Wisdom and understanding are concealed in the mind and heart, in love and fear. Torah without fear and love does not fly upward.… The small heh, the likeness of a human being, completes the four-letter Name; it is the holy kingdom, the mitzvah, the performance of the commandments, which rests in the 248 limbs. Concerning Torah and mitzvah it is said, “The revealed things belong to us.” Torah and mitzvah without fear and love cannot ascend and stand before yod and heh.’

paragraphs.text: Rema, Orach Chaim 1:1: ‘“I have set the Lord before me always” is a great principle of Torah and of the virtues of the righteous who walk before God. A person’s sitting, movements, and occupations when alone at home are not like his sitting, movements, and occupations before a great king.… All the more so when a person takes to heart that the great King, the Holy One, blessed be He, whose glory fills the whole earth, stands over him and sees his actions, as it says, “Can a person hide in concealed places and I not see him? declares the Lord.” Immediately there will come to him fear, submission in dread of God, and continual shame before Him.’

paragraphs.text: Tur, Orach Chaim 5: When reciting his blessings, he should intend the meaning of the words he utters. When mentioning the Name, he should intend the meaning of its reading with alef and dalet: lordship, for He is Master of all. He should also intend the meaning of its writing with yod and heh: existence, for He was, is, and will be. When mentioning Elokim, he should intend that He is strong and mighty, possessing power over those above and those below, for El denotes power and strength, as in: "He took the mighty men of the land."

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 50a: ‘“And His Name shall be one.” What does “one” mean? Is His Name not one now? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: The World to Come is not like this world. In this world it is written with yod and heh and read with alef and dalet; in the World to Come it will all be one, both read with yod and heh and written with yod and heh. Rava thought to expound this publicly. An elder told him: It is written “to be concealed.” Rabbi Avina raised a contradiction: It is written, “This is My Name forever,” and, “This is My remembrance for every generation.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said: I am not read as I am written. I am written with yod and heh, but read with alef and dalet.’

paragraphs.text: Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 3:5: The corresponding passage is numbered chapter 3 in this edition; the Hebrew text’s chapter 10 reference is preserved. ‘The Holy One, blessed be He, immediately consulted the Torah, whose name is Tushiyah, concerning the creation of the world. It answered Him: Master of the worlds, if a king has no army and no camp, over whom does he reign? And if there is no people to praise the king, what is the king’s glory? The Master of the world heard this, and it pleased Him. The Torah said: The Holy One, blessed be He, consulted me in creating the world, as it says, “Counsel and sound wisdom are mine.”’

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 110a, Raya Mehemna, Behar: ‘So too, the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence, although they are like souls in relation to the throne and angels, are in relation to You, the Cause of causes, like a body: You unite them and bring them close.… You are the Soul of souls; there is no soul above You and no god above You. You are outside everything, within everything, on every side, above everything, and below everything.… You bring the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence close in every sefirah and in all the branches of light that depend on them.… You have no body, no limbs, and no female counterpart, but are One without a second.’ Zohar III 110a, Raya Mehemna, Behar: ‘A king whose servants, governors, and rulers of the kingdom sent him many gifts said: Whoever wishes to send me a gift should send it only through the queen, to fulfill in her, “His kingdom rules over all.” Therefore the Divine Presence is called “an offering to the Lord,” “a burnt offering to the Lord,” and “a guilt offering to the Lord.”… All must be brought to the Lord and His Divine Presence; afterward she distributes to everyone.… Everything returns to Him. Therefore, “One who sacrifices to gods shall be proscribed, except to the Lord alone”: one must not grant authority to the Other Side through an offering, for all other gods belong to the world of separation; they possess neither closeness nor unification.’

paragraphs.text: Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah 3: ‘David the king, of blessed memory, further said: I feared out of my joy, and rejoiced out of my fear; my love rose above them all. Therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, made a covenant with me that I should be proficient in Scripture and Mishnah, in laws and aggados, as it says, “For is not my house so with God? For He has established an everlasting covenant with me, ordered in all things and guarded.” “Covenant” means none other than Torah, as it says, “My covenant was with him, life and peace.” “Ordered in all things”—in Scripture, Mishnah, laws, and aggados; “guarded”—that words of Torah should be guarded within me forever and ever.’

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 88a: ‘Rabbi Elazar said: What is meant by, “Many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us ascend to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Jacob”? The God of Jacob, and not the God of Abraham and Isaac? Rather, not like Abraham, in whose case it is called a mountain, as it says, “On the mountain of the Lord He shall be seen”; and not like Isaac, in whose case it is called a field, as it says, “Isaac went out to meditate in the field”; but like Jacob, who called it a house, as it says, “He called the name of that place Beis El.”’

paragraphs.text: Taanis 5b: ‘After they had eaten, he told him: Thus said Rabbi Yochanan: Our father Jacob did not die. He replied: Was it then for nothing that the mourners mourned, the embalmers embalmed, and the buriers buried? paragraphs.text: Eruvin 21b: Rav Yehudah said in Shmuel’s name: ‘When Solomon instituted eruvin and handwashing, a heavenly voice proclaimed: “My son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will rejoice”; and, “Be wise, my son, and gladden my heart, that I may answer him who taunts me,” etc.’ Rav Hamnuna said: ‘What does “He spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered one thousand and five” mean? It teaches that Solomon supplied three thousand parables for every matter of Torah, and one thousand and five explanations for every matter instituted by the Sages.’ Rava expounded: ‘What does “Besides being wise, Koheles also taught the people knowledge; he weighed, investigated, and arranged many proverbs” mean? “He taught the people knowledge”: he taught them through mnemonic signs and explained matters through comparable examples.’ Regarding “He weighed and investigated and arranged many proverbs,” Ulla said in Rabbi Eliezer’s name: ‘At first the Torah resembled a basket without handles, until Solomon came and made handles for it.’

paragraphs.text: Shir HaShirim Rabbah, Introduction 8: ‘Rabbi Yosi said: It resembled a large basket full of fruit that had no handle and could not be carried. A clever man came and made handles for it, and it began to be carried by its handles. So, before Solomon arose, no one could comprehend the words of Torah; when Solomon arose, everyone began to understand Torah.… Rabbi Chanina said: It resembled a deep well full of water, whose water was cool, sweet, and good, yet no creature could drink from it. A man came, joined rope to rope and cord to cord, drew water, and drank; then everyone began to draw and drink. Thus, from one matter to another and from one parable to another, Solomon came to understand the secret of Torah.… The Sages said: Do not regard this parable lightly, for through a parable a person can grasp the words of Torah. It resembles a king who lost a gold coin or a precious pearl in his house: does he not find it by means of a wick worth an issar? So do not regard a parable lightly, for through a parable a person grasps the words of Torah.’

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 13a: Rav Yehudah said in Shmuel’s name, citing Rabbi Meir: ‘When I studied under Rabbi Akiva, I would put vitriol into the ink, and he said nothing to me. When I came to Rabbi Yishmael, he asked: “My son, what is your occupation?” I answered: “I am a scribe.” He said: “My son, be careful in your work, for your work is the work of Heaven. Should you omit or add a single letter, you would destroy the entire world.” I told him: “I have a substance called vitriol, which I put into the ink.” He said: “May vitriol be put into ink? Does the Torah not say, ‘He shall write and erase’—writing that can be erased?”’ What was Rabbi Yishmael saying, and what was Rabbi Meir answering? Rabbi Meir meant: ‘Not only am I proficient and therefore do not err by omitting or adding letters; even the possibility that a fly might settle on the projection of a dalet, erase it, and turn it into a resh need not concern us. I have a substance called vitriol which I put into the ink.’

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 1:1: ‘Another interpretation: Amon means craftsman. The Torah says: I was the Holy One’s instrument of craftsmanship. In ordinary practice, when a mortal king builds a palace, he does not build it according to his own understanding, but according to that of a craftsman. The craftsman, too, does not build it according to his own understanding: he has plans and notebooks by which to know how to make the rooms and how to make the doorways. So the Holy One, blessed be He, looked into the Torah and created the world. The Torah said, “In the beginning God created.” “Beginning” means none other than Torah, as it says, “The Lord acquired me as the beginning of His way.”’

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 13b: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina said: ‘It is revealed and known to the One who spoke and the world came into being that no one in Rabbi Meir’s generation was his equal. Why, then, was the halachah not established in accordance with him? His colleagues could not fathom his reasoning: he would declare the impure pure and demonstrate grounds for it, and declare the pure impure and demonstrate grounds for it.’ A teaching states: ‘His name was not Rabbi Meir but Rabbi Nehorai. Why was he called Rabbi Meir? Because he illuminated the Sages’ eyes in halachah. Nor was the other sage’s name Nehorai, but Rabbi Nechemiah; some say Rabbi Elazar ben Arach. Why was he called Nehorai? Because he enlightened the Sages’ eyes in halachah.’ Rabbi said: ‘My greater sharpness than my colleagues comes from having seen Rabbi Meir from behind. Had I seen him from the front, I would have been sharper still, as it is written: “Your eyes shall see your teacher.”’

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 20:12: ‘“The Lord God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and clothed them.” In Rabbi Meir’s Torah they found written “garments of light.” These were the garments of the first Adam, which resembled rue: broad below and narrow above. paragraphs.text: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of Songs 4:16–17: ‘From the companions: “Blessed is He who spoke and the world came into being”—this refers to the Head that is not known. “Blessed is He”—the Head of Nothingness. “Blessed is He who makes the beginning”—the Head of Arich Anpin. “Blessed is He who says and does”—Abba. “Blessed is He who decrees and fulfills”—Imma.… Through this, the flow is awakened from the primordial radiance to the Head that is not known, and from one level to the next in order.… Baruch She’amar alludes to Atzilus.… By His utterance the four worlds were made—Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah—and everything within them.… Baruch She’amar is recited standing.… For the sake of Zeir Anpin and its female counterpart, it is now sufficient that the flow come from its place as an illumination, so that the lower worlds can benefit from it; through them it reaches us.’

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 1:10: ‘What did Moses our teacher seek to apprehend when he said, “Show me, please, Your glory”? He sought to know the reality of the Holy One’s existence so that it would be known in his heart as he knows a person whose face he has seen and whose image is engraved in his heart, distinguishing that person from others.… God answered that the understanding of a living person, composed of body and soul, cannot fully apprehend the truth of this matter. He nevertheless made known to Moses what no person before him had known and no person after him would know, until Moses apprehended something of His true existence by which the Holy One was distinguished in his understanding from all other beings. This is like distinguishing from others a person whose back one has seen, apprehending his body and clothing. Scripture alludes to this in saying, “You shall see My back, but My face shall not be seen.”’

paragraphs.text: Horayos 13b recounts that, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was Nasi, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Nassan planned to embarrass him and take his place. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel punished them by directing that teachings of Rabbi Meir be cited as ‘Others say’ rather than in his name. The passage then relates: Rabbi was teaching his son Rabban Shimon: ‘Others say: Had it been a substitute offering, it would not have been offered.’ His son asked: ‘Who are these people whose waters we drink but whose names we do not mention?’ Rabbi answered: ‘People who sought to uproot your honor and the honor of your father’s house.’ His son replied: ‘Their love, their hatred, and their jealousy have already perished!’ Rabbi answered: ‘The enemy’s devastation has ended forever.’ His son replied: ‘That applies when their deeds achieved their purpose; the Sages’ deeds did not achieve their purpose.’ Rabbi then taught him: ‘They said in Rabbi Meir’s name: Had it been a substitute offering, it would not have been offered.’ Rava said: ‘Even Rabbi, who was humble, taught “They said in Rabbi Meir’s name,” but did not say “Rabbi Meir said.”’

paragraphs.text: Niddah 61b: ‘The Sages taught: A garment in which a forbidden mixture of wool and linen was lost may not be sold to a gentile or made into a donkey’s saddlecloth, but may be made into shrouds for the dead. Abaye—and some say Rav Dimi—said to him: But Rabbi Manni said in Rabbi Yannai’s name that this was taught only for eulogizing the deceased, whereas burying him in it is forbidden! He replied: Was it not stated concerning this that Rabbi Yochanan said: Even for burying him? Rabbi Yochanan follows his own reasoning, for he said: What does “free among the dead” mean? Once a person dies, he becomes free of the commandments.’

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 13b: Rabbi Abba said in Shmuel’s name: ‘For three years Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel disputed. Each maintained that the halachah followed its own rulings. A heavenly voice proclaimed: “These and those are the words of the living God, but the halachah follows Beis Hillel.” Since both are the words of the living God, why did Beis Hillel merit having the halachah established in accordance with them? Because they were gentle and forbearing, studied both their own teachings and Beis Shammai’s, and even presented Beis Shammai’s teachings before their own.’ Thus we learned: If a person’s head and most of his body are in the sukkah but his table is inside the house, Beis Shammai disqualify it and Beis Hillel permit it. Beis Hillel asked Beis Shammai: ‘Did the elders of both houses not visit Rabbi Yochanan ben HaChoranis and find him sitting with his head and most of his body in the sukkah and his table inside the house?’ Beis Shammai replied: ‘Is that a proof? They too told him: “If this was your practice, you never fulfilled the mitzvah of sukkah in your life.”’ This teaches that God elevates whoever humbles himself and humbles whoever elevates himself. Greatness flees from whoever pursues it and pursues whoever flees from it. Whoever forces the moment is pressed by the moment, while the moment stands ready for whoever yields to it.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 192b, Balak: ‘What did He do? He called Samael, who came before Him, and said to him: Do you wish to receive My Torah? He asked: What is written in it? He answered: “You shall not murder.” The Holy One, blessed be He, went directly to the point that was needed. Samael said: Heaven forbid! This Torah is Yours, and Yours it shall remain; I do not want this Torah. He returned and pleaded before Him, saying: Master of the world, if You give it to me, all my dominion will pass away, for my dominion is over killing. There will be no wars, and my dominion is over the planet Mars. If so, everything will be abolished from the world. Master of the world, take Your Torah; let me have no portion or inheritance in it.’

paragraphs.text: Bava Basra 123b: ‘Rabbi Chelbo asked Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani: It is written, “When Rachel had given birth to Joseph”—why specifically when Joseph was born? He answered: Our father Jacob saw that Esau’s descendants would be delivered only into the hands of Joseph’s descendants, as it says, “The house of Jacob shall be fire, the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau straw.” He objected: But it says of David, “He struck them from twilight until the evening of the following day”! He answered: The one who taught you the Prophets did not teach you the Writings, for it says that men from Manasseh joined David when he went to Ziklag.… Rav Yosef objected from the sons of Simeon who struck the remnant of Amalek. Rabbah bar Sheila answered: Their leader Yishi descended from Manasseh, as it says, “The sons of Manasseh: Chepher and Yishi.”’

paragraphs.text: Megillah 7a: ‘Esther sent to the Sages: Write me into Scripture for future generations. They sent back: “Have I not written for you threefold?” Threefold, and not fourfold—until they found a verse written in the Torah: “Write this as a memorial in a book.” “Write this”—what is written here and in Deuteronomy; “as a memorial”—what is written in the Prophets; “in a book”—what is written in the Megillah. This is a dispute of Tannaim: Rabbi Yehoshua assigns the three expressions to the passages in Exodus, Deuteronomy, and the Prophets; Rabbi Elazar HaModai assigns “write this” to Exodus and Deuteronomy together, “memorial” to the Prophets, and “book” to the Megillah.’

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 23b–24a: ‘Rav Yehudah said in Shmuel’s name: In these three matters the Sages are accustomed to alter their statements: a tractate, the bed, and hospitality. What practical difference does this make? Mar Zutra said: Returning a lost object to a scholar through recognition. If we know that he alters his statements only in these three matters, we return it to him; if he alters his statements in other matters, we do not return it to him.’ Rashi, Bava Metzia 23b–24a: ‘“A tractate”—if asked whether a particular tractate is well ordered in his learning, even though it is, he may answer no; this is an expression of humility. “The bed”—if asked whether he had marital relations, he may answer no; this is an expression of modesty. “Hospitality”—if asked whether his host received him graciously, he may answer no. This is a good practice, so that unsuitable people will not rush to visit the host continually and exhaust his resources.’

paragraphs.text: Beitzah 16a: ‘They said of Shammai the Elder: Throughout his life he ate in honor of Shabbos. If he found a fine animal, he would say, “This is for Shabbos.” If he found another finer than the first, he reserved the second and ate the first. Hillel the Elder had a different practice: all his deeds were for the sake of Heaven, as it is written, “Blessed is the Lord, day by day.” It was likewise taught: Beis Shammai say, “From the first day of the week, prepare for your Shabbos”; Beis Hillel say, “Blessed is the Lord, day by day.”’ Vayikra Rabbah 34:3: ‘“A man of kindness benefits his own soul”—this is Hillel the Elder. When he parted from his students, he walked along with them. They asked: Our master, where are you going? He answered: To perform a mitzvah. What mitzvah? To bathe in the bathhouse. Is this a mitzvah? He answered: Yes. If the person appointed to clean and wash the statues of kings receives sustenance and distinction among the royal dignitaries, then I, who was created in the Divine image and likeness, all the more so!… Another interpretation: Hillel said to his students: I am going to do kindness for the guest in my house. They asked: Do you have a guest every day? He answered: Is this poor soul not a guest within the body? Today it is here; tomorrow it is no longer here.’

paragraphs.text: Zohar I 11a, Introduction: ‘In the morning, when a person rises from his bed, he should bless his Master, enter His house, and bow before His sanctuary with great fear; afterward he should pray and take counsel from the holy patriarchs, as it says, “Through Your abundant kindness I shall enter Your house; I shall bow toward Your holy sanctuary in fear of You.” They explained: A person should not enter the synagogue before taking counsel with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, for they instituted prayer before the Holy One. “Through Your abundant kindness I shall enter Your house”—Abraham; “I shall bow toward Your holy sanctuary”—Isaac; “in fear of You”—Jacob. He must first include them, and afterward enter the synagogue and pray.’

paragraphs.text: Yevamos 65b: ‘Rabbi Ile’a said in Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon’s name: A person may alter his words for the sake of peace, as it says, “Your father commanded … thus shall you say to Joseph: Please forgive.” Rabbi Nassan says: It is a mitzvah, as it says, “Samuel said: How can I go? Saul will hear and kill me.” The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: Great is peace, for even the Holy One altered His words for its sake. Originally Sarah said, “My husband is old”; afterward God reported her words as, “I have grown old.” Vayikra Rabbah 9:9, concluding discourse on peace: ‘Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai said: Great is peace, for all blessings are included in it.… Rabbi Mani of Sha’ab and Rabbi Yehoshua of Sikhnin said in Rabbi Levi’s name: Great is peace, for all the blessings, good things, and consolations that the Holy One brings upon Israel conclude with peace. In the Shema: “Who spreads the shelter of peace”; in prayer: “Who makes peace”; in the priestly blessing: “May He grant you peace.”… The Sages said: Great is peace, for when King Mashiach comes, he opens only with peace, as it says, “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace.”’ Midrash Tanchuma, Tzav 7: ‘In the World to Come, when the Holy One returns the exiles to Jerusalem, He returns them in peace, as it says, “Seek the peace of Jerusalem; may those who love you be tranquil.” It also says, “Behold, I shall extend peace to her like a river.”’

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 8:5: ‘Rabbi Simon said: When the Holy One came to create the first man, the ministering angels formed groups and companies. Some said, “Let him not be created,” and others said, “Let him be created.” Thus it is written, “Kindness and truth met; righteousness and peace kissed.” Kindness said: Let him be created, for he performs acts of kindness. Truth said: Let him not be created, for he is entirely falsehood. Righteousness said: Let him be created, for he performs righteous deeds. Peace said: Let him not be created, for he is entirely strife. What did the Holy One do? He took truth and cast it to the earth, as it says, “You cast truth to the earth.” The ministering angels said before Him: Master of the world, why do You disparage Your own royal insignia? Let truth rise from the earth, as it says, “Truth shall sprout from the earth.”… While the ministering angels were still debating with one another, the Holy One created man. He said: Why are you debating? Man has already been made.’

paragraphs.text: Sukkah 28a: ‘If a person’s head and most of his body were in the sukkah, but his table was inside the house, Beis Shammai disqualify it and Beis Hillel permit it. Beis Hillel said to Beis Shammai: Was there not an incident in which the elders of Beis Shammai and the elders of Beis Hillel visited Rabbi Yochanan ben HaChoranis, found him sitting with his head and most of his body in the sukkah and his table inside the house, and said nothing to him? Beis Shammai replied: Is that a proof? They too said to him: If this was your practice, you never fulfilled the mitzvah of sukkah in your life.’

paragraphs.text: Berachos 31b–32a: ‘Rabbi Elazar said: Elijah directed forceful words toward Heaven, as it says, “You have turned their hearts backward.” Rabbi Shmuel bar Rabbi Yitzchak said: From where do we know that the Holy One afterward acknowledged Elijah’s claim? For it is written, “whom I have harmed.” Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina said: Were it not for these three verses, the feet of Israel’s enemies would have collapsed: “whom I have harmed”; “Like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand, house of Israel”; and “I shall remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.” Rav Pappa said: From this verse, “I shall place My spirit within you and bring it about that you walk in My statutes.”’

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 89b: ‘God said to Isaac: Your children have sinned against Me. Isaac answered: Master of the world, are they my children and not Your children? When they placed “we shall do” before “we shall hear,” You called them “My firstborn son”; now are they my children and not Your children? Moreover, how much have they sinned? A person’s years are seventy. Subtract twenty, for which You do not punish them, leaving fifty. Subtract twenty-five for the nights, leaving twenty-five. Subtract twelve and a half for prayer, eating, and the privy, leaving twelve and a half. If You bear all of it, good; otherwise, half shall be upon me and half upon You. If You say that all shall be upon me, I already offered myself before You.’

paragraphs.text: Shir HaShirim Rabbah, Introduction 9: ‘Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair used to say: Diligence leads to cleanliness; cleanliness to purity; purity to holiness; holiness to humility; humility to fear of sin; fear of sin to piety; piety to divine inspiration; divine inspiration to resurrection; and resurrection to Elijah the prophet, remembered for good.… Humility leads to fear of sin, as it says, “At the heel of humility is fear of the Lord.”… Rabbi Mattana said: What wisdom made a crown for its head, humility made a sandal for its heel. paragraphs.text: Zohar III 97a–97b, Emor: ‘When Israel were in Egypt, they were under another dominion and attached to impurity, like a woman during her days of impurity. After they were circumcised, they entered the holy portion called the covenant. When they attached themselves to it, their impurity ceased, like a woman whose impure blood has ceased. After it ceases, what is written? “She shall count seven days for herself.” Here too, once they entered the holy portion and their impurity ceased, the Holy One said: From now onward, count toward purity. “You shall count for yourselves”—specifically for yourselves, just as “she shall count for herself” means for herself. Why? To become purified in the holy supernal waters, and afterward to unite with the King and receive His Torah. There it says seven days; here, seven weeks—to merit purification in the waters of the flowing river, called living waters, from which the seven weeks emerge.’ Zohar III 97a, Raya Mehemna, Emor: ‘Although Israel had become purified to observe Pesach and had emerged from impurity, they were not yet complete and purified as they should be.… Like a woman who emerges from impurity and then begins to count, so Israel, after leaving Egypt, emerged from impurity and observed Pesach to eat at their Father’s table. From then onward they must count, bringing the woman near her husband and uniting with him. These are fifty days of purity, to enter the mystery of the World to Come and receive the Torah.… These fifty are forty-nine, encompassing the aspects of Torah; the fiftieth day is the mystery of Torah itself.’

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 5:5: ‘Perhaps you will say: Does not the Holy One know everything that will be? Before a person existed, did He know that this person would be righteous or wicked, or did He not know? If He knew that he would be righteous, it is impossible for him not to be righteous. If you say that He knew he would be righteous but he could nevertheless be wicked, then He did not know the matter with certainty! Know that the answer to this question is longer than the earth and wider than the sea, and many great principles and lofty mountains depend upon it. But you must know and understand what I say: We have already explained that the Holy One does not know through knowledge outside Himself, as people do, for they and their knowledge are two things. Rather, He and His knowledge are one, and human understanding cannot fully apprehend this. Just as a person cannot apprehend the Creator’s true reality, so a person cannot apprehend the Creator’s knowledge, as the prophet said, “My thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not My ways.” Therefore we cannot know how the Holy One knows all creatures and deeds. Yet we know without doubt that a person’s deeds are in his own hands: the Holy One does not draw him along or decree that he act in a particular way. This is known through clear proofs of wisdom, and not only through the received faith. Therefore prophecy says that a person is judged for his deeds, according to whether they are good or bad. This is the principle upon which all the words of prophecy depend.’

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Mikvaos 11:12: ‘It is clear and evident that impurity and purity are decrees of Scripture. They are not matters decided by human reasoning, but are among the statutes. Immersion from impurity is likewise among the statutes, for impurity is not mud or filth that water removes; it is a decree of Scripture, and the matter depends upon the intention of the heart. Therefore the Sages said: If someone immersed without establishing the required intention, it is as though he did not immerse. Nevertheless, there is an allusion in this: Just as one who directs his heart toward purification becomes pure upon immersing, although nothing in his body has changed, so one who directs his heart toward purifying his soul from the impurities of the soul—wrongful thoughts and evil opinions—becomes pure once he resolves in his heart to separate from those counsels and brings his soul into the waters of knowledge. Thus it says, “I shall sprinkle pure water upon you, and you shall become pure; from all your impurities and from all your idols I shall purify you.” May God, in His abundant mercy, purify us from every sin, iniquity, and guilt. Amen.’

paragraphs.text: Sefer HaChinuch 173: ‘Concerning why water purifies every impure person, I think, on the plain level, that the purpose is for a person to see himself after immersion as though he had been created at that moment, just as the entire world was water before there was a human being in it, as it says, “The spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.” Through this image he should take to heart that, just as his body has been renewed, he should renew his actions for good, improve his deeds, and attend carefully to God’s ways. Therefore the Sages said that purification is not valid in water in a vessel, but only in spring water or collected water upon the ground, outside a vessel, so that he may imagine that the entire world is water and that he is renewed upon emerging. If the water is in a vessel, or even passed through a vessel, this thought cannot properly arise: everything in a vessel made by human hands has a boundary, and he will not think of the entire world as water, as at the beginning, and of himself as newly created.’

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 39b: ‘Rava said: This follows Rabbi Yaakov, who says that there is no reward for a mitzvah in this world. Rabbi Yaakov taught: Every mitzvah whose reward is written beside it in the Torah refers to the resurrection of the dead. Concerning honoring parents it says, “So that your days may be prolonged and so that it may be good for you”; concerning sending away the mother bird, “So that it may be good for you and you may prolong your days.” If a father told his son to climb a building and bring him young birds, and the son climbed, sent away the mother, took the young, and fell and died on his return—where are his good days and prolonged days? paragraphs.text: Tosafos, Eruvin 21a, “One part in three thousand two hundred of the Torah”: ‘In the poem “Then You saw and counted,” Rabbi Elazar HaKalir gives two thousand four hundred for the world in relation to the Torah’s length. This is because he treats a span as one third of a cubit, as he writes that the span extends to two finger-spreads, and that four fingerbreadths make a handbreadth and a finger-spread. According to the calculation in our passage, however, a span is half a cubit, and every cubit divided lengthwise and crosswise contains four square spans. Yet his calculation is difficult: he should divide a square cubit into nine parts, each a span by a span, for the world is a span by a span; the result would then be seven thousand two hundred. Instead, he treats the world as a span by a cubit—what is his source for that?’

paragraphs.text: Rashba, Toras HaBayis HaAroch 4:1, parallel passage on a whole creature: ‘Among the things that are not nullified is an intrinsically forbidden whole creature. Nevertheless, it is not like the other forbidden things of which we said that they are never nullified: this is nullified in nine hundred and sixty, as I shall explain below. Until that ratio, it is not nullified.… Rabbeinu Shimshon wrote that the Yerushalmi explains the ratio as one in nine hundred and sixty. The Yerushalmi says that Rabbi Yosi ruled in Akhbara according to one in a thousand: he found one in a thousand and permitted it. Rabbeinu Shimshon wrote that he would likewise have permitted it at nine hundred and sixty; the reason such a large ratio is required is that a whole creature is not nullified. From here we learn that, although we say a whole creature is not nullified, it is nullified in nine hundred and sixty. This cannot be used to infer the rule for the other prohibitions that forbid a mixture in any quantity, such as something that will become permitted, for they said that such a thing is not nullified even in a thousand.’

paragraphs.text: Tosafos, Pesachim 109b, “In the sea that Solomon made”: ‘The Yerushalmi asks: Was its water not drawn water? Although a vessel holding forty se’ah of liquid, corresponding to two kor of dry material, does not receive impurity because it cannot be moved both full and empty, it is nevertheless a vessel for the law of drawn water.… Moreover, Solomon’s sea was made of copper and could receive impurity even though it could not be moved full and empty; only wooden utensils were compared to a sack. The answer is: The feet of the oxen supporting it had holes large enough for a pomegranate to pass through, and they were connected to the spring beneath them. The pomegranate-sized holes removed the oxen’s status as utensils, so that they would not receive impurity; for making the sea’s water valid, a hole the size of a waterskin’s tube would suffice.… My teacher Rabbi Yechiel explained that pomegranate-sized holes were needed here because the oxen intervened between the sea and the spring, with considerable distance between them; the water therefore had to enter abundantly.’

paragraphs.text: Menachos 29b: ‘Rabbi Yehudah son of Rabbi Ilai expounded: These are the two worlds that the Holy One, blessed be He, created—one with heh and one with yod. I do not know whether the World to Come was created with yod and this world with heh, or the reverse. When Scripture says, “These are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created,” do not read “when they were created,” but “He created them with heh.” Why was this world created with heh? Because it resembles a portico, so that anyone who wishes to leave can leave. Why is its leg suspended? So that if a person returns in repentance, they may bring him in.… One who comes to purify himself is assisted; one who comes to make himself impure is given an opening.… Why was the World to Come created with yod? Because the righteous in it are few. Why is its head bent? Because the righteous in it bow their heads on account of their deeds, which are not alike.’

paragraphs.text: Shemot Rabbah 47:8: How did Moses know how many days he had spent there? It is written: “He was there with the Lord forty days and forty nights.” ... When God spoke with him, Moses stood; when He withdrew from him, Moses sat and reviewed what he had learned. Thus both “I stood on the mountain” and “I sat on the mountain” are fulfilled. When God spoke with him, he knew it was day; when He told him, “Study your Torah,” he knew it was night. Yedei Moshe on Shemot Rabbah 47:8: “How did Moses know how many days he had spent on the mountain?” The question is asked: perhaps in heaven he did not know, and only afterward, when he came down, did he know how many days he had spent there. It appears that this refers to the earlier teaching of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: one should study the Written Torah specifically by day and the Oral Torah by night. Presumably Moses also acted in accordance with this rule. The question is therefore how he knew when it was night. The answer is: when God spoke with him—the Written Torah—he knew it was day; when He said, “Study your Torah”—the Oral Torah—he knew it was night.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 8:2: “Rav Chama bar Chanina opened: ‘Have you known this from of old?’ Rabbi Chama bar Chanina said: This resembles a city supplied by donkey drivers. They would ask one another: What grain business was done in the city today? Those arriving on the sixth day asked those from the fifth; those from the fifth asked those from the fourth; those from the fourth asked those from the third; those from the third asked those from the second; and those from the second asked those from the first. Whom could those from the first ask? Could they not ask the townspeople who were engaged in building the city? Likewise, the creations of each day asked one another: What creatures did the Holy One, blessed be He, create among you? The sixth day asked the fifth, and so on back to the first. paragraphs.text: Sotah 21a: “For a commandment is a lamp, and Torah is light.” Just as a lamp protects only for a time, so a commandment protects only for a time; just as light protects continually, so Torah protects continually. It is like a person walking in the darkness of night, afraid of thorns, pits, briars, wild animals, and robbers, and not knowing which road he is on. A torch saves him from the thorns, pits, and briars, but he still fears wild animals and robbers and does not know his road. When dawn breaks, he is saved from wild animals and robbers, but still does not know his road. When he reaches a crossroads, he is saved from them all. Another interpretation: a transgression extinguishes a commandment, but does not extinguish Torah.

paragraphs.text: Tosafot on Sukkah 13a, “With three it is called a bundle”: This is difficult, for the passage in Avot appears to imply that fewer than five are not called a bundle: “From where do we know that even five [who study Torah have the Divine Presence among them]? ‘He founded His band upon the earth.’” Some texts reverse the derivations, deriving five from “in the midst” and three from “His band.” ... Perhaps, although a bundle generally consists of three, this verse, “He founded His band upon the earth,” applies specifically to five, since it is written, “My hand also founded the earth,” and a hand has five fingers. Tosafot on Sukkah 13a, “The commandment of hyssop is three stalks”: “There is no bundle of fewer than three.”

paragraphs.text: Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed III:32: “It is impossible to pass suddenly from one extreme to the other; human nature will not allow a person suddenly to abandon everything to which he has been accustomed. ... The manner of worship then generally practiced, in which people had been brought up, consisted of sacrificing animals in temples containing images, bowing to those images, and burning incense before them. His wisdom did not require us to abandon all these forms of worship, for accepting such a command would have been contrary to human nature, which always inclines toward what it is accustomed to. ... God transferred these forms of service to Himself: He commanded us to build a sanctuary for Him, to erect an altar to His name, and to offer the sacrifices to Him. ... Through this divine plan the traces of idolatry were effaced, and the great foundation of our faith—the existence and unity of God—was established.”

Impurity is not mud or filth which water can remove; it is a decree of Scripture, and the matter depends on the intention of the heart. ... The wicked are judged by it, as it is written: ‘Behold, the day comes, burning like an oven; all the arrogant and all who do wickedness will be straw, and the coming day will burn them.’ ... The righteous are healed by it, as it is written: ‘For you who fear My name, the sun of righteousness shall shine, with healing in its wings.’ Moreover, they delight in it, as it is said: ‘You shall go forth and frisk like calves of the stall.’”

paragraphs.text: Peri HaAretz, Lech Lecha, paragraph beginning “Our Sages said: Circumcision in that place”: “When a person reaches attachment [to God], he will understand through his faith that he has not yet attained even a trace or the slightest edge of comprehension of Him, and has not entered into it at all. His glory is his faith alone: to attach himself to Him through faith after all the investigations and intellectual attainments he has achieved. All his attainments cannot encompass Him, for He is infinite, blessed be He. Rather, all his attainments serve only to strengthen faith. ... Abraham recognized his Creator at three years of age through investigation and contemplation, and continued to grow in knowledge, understanding, and intellect. After all this he was wholehearted in his deeds, which is faith alone. ... True connection and attachment to Him are through this faith alone.”

paragraphs.text: Zohar III, Behar 108a (Behar 3:1–2): “What is the yoke of the kingdom of heaven? It is like an ox upon which a yoke is first placed, so that it may bring benefit to the world. If it does not accept that yoke, it does nothing. So too a person must first accept the yoke, and afterward serve through it in all that is required. If he does not first accept it, he cannot serve. This is what is written: ‘Serve the Lord with fear.’ What is ‘with fear’? As you say: ‘The beginning of wisdom is fear of the Lord.’ This is the kingdom of heaven. ... Therefore it comes before everything. What proves this? Tefillin: first the one on the arm, for through this he enters the remaining holiness.”

paragraphs.text: Tanya, Likkutei Amarim 41: “With this preparation of giving his soul to God, a person should begin the morning blessings, ‘Blessed are You ...’ With this preparation, too, he should begin to study a fixed portion immediately after prayer. Likewise, in the middle of the day, before beginning to study, at least this preparation is necessary. As is known, the essential preparation for study for its own sake, which is indispensable, is at the beginning of study for the intermediate person. This is like a bill of divorce and a Torah scroll, for which the intention of writing for their particular purpose is indispensable, yet it suffices to say at the beginning of the writing: ‘I am writing for the sanctity of a Torah scroll,’ or ‘for him and for her.’ When studying many hours continuously, one should reflect upon this preparation at least every hour.”

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 30b: Rav Yehudah son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilat said in Rav’s name: “The Sages wished to put away the book of Kohelet because its statements contradict one another. Why did they not put it away? Because its beginning is words of Torah and its end is words of Torah. Its beginning is words of Torah, as it is written: ‘What profit does a person have from all his labor which he labors under the sun?’ The school of Rabbi Yannai said: ‘Under the sun he has none; before the sun he has [profit].’ Its end is words of Torah, as it is written: ‘The end of the matter, all having been heard: fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole of man.’”

paragraphs.text: Maharal, Netivot Olam, Netiv HaEmunah 2: “In the midrash: ‘Then Moses sang’—‘They believed in the Lord,’ and therefore merited to inherit the Land. You find that through the faith with which our father Abraham believed, he inherited this world and the World to Come, as it is said: ‘He believed in the Lord, and He accounted it to him as righteousness.’ ... The midrash wishes to explain how great faith is before the Holy One, blessed be He, for one who believes in Him attaches himself to Him, and this reaches without limit or end. ... The exiles are gathered, to become wholly attached to Him and leave the dominion of the nations, only through faith. When Israel’s faith is firmly rooted in Him, such a nation should not be in exile, wandering from place to place. Therefore the exiles are gathered to be planted with God, in accordance with the nature of faith.”

paragraphs.text: Tikkunei Zohar, Second Introduction, “Patach Eliyahu,” 17a: Eliyahu opened and said: “Master of the worlds, You are One, but not in a numerical reckoning. You are exalted above all the exalted, hidden beyond all that is hidden. No thought grasps You at all. You brought forth ten arrangements, which we call ten sefirot, through which to govern hidden worlds that are not revealed and worlds that are revealed. Through them You conceal Yourself from human beings. You bind them and unite them; because You are within them, whoever separates one of these ten from another is considered as though he separated within You. ... Malchut is the mouth; we call it the Oral Torah. Chokhmah is the brain, the inner thought. Binah is the heart, and through it the heart understands. Concerning these two it is written: ‘The hidden things belong to the Lord our God.’”

paragraphs.text: Berachos 11b: What is the other blessing [before the Shema]? Rav Yehudah said in Shmuel’s name: “‘Abundant love.’” Rabbi Elazar likewise instructed his son Rabbi Pedat: “‘Abundant love.’” A baraita also teaches: “One does not say ‘Everlasting love,’ but ‘Abundant love.’” The sages say: “‘Everlasting love,’ as it is said: ‘I have loved you with everlasting love; therefore I have drawn you with kindness.’” Rav Yehudah said in Shmuel’s name: “One who rises early to study, before reciting the Shema, must recite a blessing. After reciting the Shema, he need not recite a blessing, for he has already fulfilled his obligation through ‘Abundant love.’”

paragraphs.text: Berachos 14b: A baraita teaches that Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says: “It is fitting that ‘Hear, O Israel’ precede ‘And it shall be, if you listen,’ for this concerns learning and that concerns teaching; and that ‘And it shall be, if you listen’ precede ‘And the Lord said,’ for this concerns learning and that concerns doing.” Does ‘Hear, O Israel’ contain learning but no teaching or doing? It is written: “You shall teach them,” “You shall bind them,” and “You shall write them”! Furthermore, does ‘And it shall be, if you listen’ contain teaching but no doing? It is written: “You shall bind them” and “You shall write them”! Rather, this is what he means: “‘Hear, O Israel’ should precede ‘And it shall be, if you listen,’ because it contains learning, teaching, and doing. ‘And it shall be, if you listen’ should precede ‘And the Lord said,’ because it contains teaching and doing, while ‘And the Lord said’ contains only doing.”

paragraphs.text: Asarah Maamarot, Maamar Chikur Din, III:11: “The first commandment we have mentioned is a model for all the commandments, which require much watchfulness and preparation, as King Solomon, of blessed memory, proclaimed: ‘One who keeps a commandment will know no evil thing.’ Learn this from the eating of the Passover offering in Egypt, of which Scripture speaks of the haste of the Divine Presence, which hastened to redeem its children. To warn against confusion and turmoil in performing that commandment, and to teach us that haste is stated only with this intention, Scripture first explained, ‘Thus shall you eat it,’ with three forms of preparation. It is known from the words of the sages that a transgression for its own sake is greater than a commandment performed for an ulterior motive.”

paragraphs.text: Berachos 46a–46b: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta said in Rav’s name: “Know that ‘Who is good and does good’ is not ordained by the Torah, for one begins it with ‘Blessed’ and does not conclude it with ‘Blessed.’” As a baraita teaches: “All blessings begin with ‘Blessed’ and conclude with ‘Blessed,’ except the blessing over fruit, blessings over commandments, a blessing adjacent to another blessing, and the final blessing of the Shema. paragraphs.text: Berachos 2a: "To what earlier subject is the tanna referring when he teaches, 'From when'? Furthermore, why does he teach the evening Shema first? Let him teach the morning Shema first! The tanna refers to the verse, 'When you lie down and when you rise,' and teaches as follows: When is the time for reciting Shema associated with lying down? From when the kohanim enter to eat their terumah. Alternatively, he derives it from the creation of the world, as it is written: 'There was evening and there was morning, one day.' If so, in the later clause, which teaches, 'In the morning one recites two blessings before it and one after it; in the evening, two before it and two after it,' let him teach the evening first! The tanna began with the evening and then taught the morning. While dealing with the morning, he explained the matters of the morning, and afterward explained the matters of the evening."

paragraphs.text: Sefer HaChinukh 417, The Unity of God: “We are commanded to believe that God, blessed be He, brings all existence into being, is Master of all, and is One without any partner, as it is said: ‘Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One.’ This is a positive commandment, not merely a statement. ‘Hear’ means: receive this from me, know it, and believe it—that God, who is our God, is One. ... This is one of the commandments mentioned at the beginning of the book that a person must fulfill constantly: its obligation never ceases, even for a brief moment.” Sefer HaChinukh 418, Love of God: “It is fitting that a person direct all his thought and purpose toward love of God, and always consider in his heart that all worldly wealth, children, and honor are as nothing, naught, and emptiness in comparison with love of Him, blessed be He. He should labor continually, all day, in seeking wisdom, so as to attain knowledge of Him. In the end, he should do everything he can to accustom the thoughts of his heart throughout the day to belief in Him and His unity, until there is not a single moment, by day or night while awake, when he does not remember the love of his Master with all his heart. ... This is one of the constant commandments incumbent upon a person forever.”

paragraphs.text: Rema on Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 1:1: “‘I have set the Lord before me always’ is a great principle in the Torah and in the virtues of the righteous who walk before God. A person’s sitting, movements, and occupations when alone in his house are unlike his sitting, movements, and occupations before a great king. Nor is his speech and freedom to speak as he wishes among his household and relatives like his speech in the king’s presence. All the more so, when a person takes to heart that the great King, the Holy One, blessed be He, whose glory fills the whole earth, stands over him and sees his deeds—as it is said: ‘If a person hides in secret places, shall I not see him? says the Lord’—fear and submission in dread of God immediately come upon him, and he is always ashamed before Him. ... Even when walking discreetly and lying upon his bed, he should know before Whom he lies; and as soon as he awakens from sleep, he should rise eagerly for the service of his Creator, blessed and exalted be He.”

paragraphs.text: Berachos 2a–b: The Mishnah teaches when priests may eat terumah, and thereby teaches “that atonement does not prevent [them from eating it]. As it was taught: ‘And the sun sets, and it is clear’—the setting of his sun prevents him from eating terumah, but his atonement does not prevent him from eating terumah.” Rabbah bar Rav Sheila explains: “If so, the verse should say, ‘And he shall become pure.’ What does ‘and it is clear’ mean? The day has become clear, as people say: ‘The sun has set and the day has cleared away.’” The Gemara confirms this from the baraisa’s sign, the appearance of the stars: “It refers to the setting of the sun, and ‘and it is clear’ means the day has become clear.” Yevamos 74b: “He immersed and emerged—he may eat second tithe. His sun set—he may eat terumah. He brought his atonement offering—he may eat sacrificial food.” Rava said in Rav Chisda’s name: “Three verses are written. It is written: ‘He shall not eat of the sacred things unless he has washed his flesh in water’—thus, if he has washed, he is pure. And it is written: ‘And the sun sets, and it is clear; afterward he may eat of the sacred things.’ And it is written: ‘The priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be pure.’ How can this be? Here [the first verse applies] to second tithe; here [the second] to terumah; here [the third] to sacrificial food.”

paragraphs.text: Berachos 3a: Rabbi Eliezer teaches: ‘The night has three watches. During each watch God sits and roars like a lion, as it is written: “The Lord shall roar from on high, and give forth His voice from His holy dwelling; He shall roar mightily over His habitation.” Their signs are: in the first watch, a donkey brays; in the second, dogs bark; in the third, an infant nurses from its mother’s breasts and a woman speaks with her husband.’ The passage later explains why a sign is needed for the end of the third watch, although dawn itself marks its end: ‘It enables someone sleeping in a dark house, who does not know when the time for Shema arrives, to recite Shema. When a woman speaks with her husband and an infant nurses, let him rise and recite it.’ Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel said in Rav’s name: ‘The night has three watches. During each one God sits and roars like a lion, saying: “Woe to the children because of whose sins I destroyed My house, burned My sanctuary, and exiled them among the nations.”’

When a woman speaks with her husband and an infant nurses, let him rise and recite it.’ Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel said in Rav’s name: ‘The night has three watches. During each one God sits and roars like a lion, saying: “Woe to the children because of whose sins I destroyed My house, burned My sanctuary, and exiled them among the nations.”’

paragraphs.text: Berachos 2a: “From when does one recite the Shema in the evening? From when the priests enter to eat their terumah, until the end of the first watch; these are Rabbi Eliezer’s words. Once his sons returned from a feast and said to him: ‘We have not recited the Shema.’ He said to them: ‘If dawn has not risen, you are obligated to recite it.’ ... paragraphs.text: Berachos 26b: “Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina said: The Patriarchs instituted the prayers. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: The prayers were instituted corresponding to the daily offerings.” A baraisa supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: “Why did they say that the morning prayer may be recited until noon? Because the morning daily offering may be brought until noon.” ... “Why did they say that the afternoon prayer may be recited until evening? Because the afternoon daily offering may be brought until evening.” ... “Why did they say that the evening prayer has no fixed time? Because limbs and fats that were not consumed in the evening continue to be offered throughout the night.” The Gemara explains Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina’s position: “The Patriarchs instituted the prayers, and the Sages aligned them with the offerings.”

paragraphs.text: Ta’anit 7a: Rabbi Chanina bar Idi said: “Why are words of Torah compared to water, as it is written: ‘Everyone who thirsts, come to the water’? To teach you: Just as water leaves a high place and goes to a low place, so words of Torah endure only in one whose mind is humble.” Rabbi Oshaya said: “Why are words of Torah compared to these three liquids—water, wine, and milk—as it is written: ‘Everyone who thirsts, come to the water,’ and ‘Come, buy and eat; come, buy wine and milk without money and without price’? To teach you: Just as these three liquids keep only in the least costly vessels, so words of Torah endure only in one whose mind is humble.”

paragraphs.text: Zohar I, Bereshit 23b (Bereshit 17:4–6): “David, on account of the exile, said: ‘Hungry, weary, and thirsty in the wilderness.’ Because he saw the Shechinah desolate and dry, he bore sorrow for her. After he saw Israel returning in joy, he instituted ten kinds of song. At the end of them all he said: ‘A prayer of the poor person when he wraps himself.’ This is the prayer that envelops all the prayers before it until its own prayer enters. Therefore the poor person precedes them all. What is the prayer of the poor person? It is the evening prayer, which is in a domain of her own, without her husband; because she is without her husband, she is poor and dry. ... Therefore a person must be like a poor person at the King’s gate during the Amidah on all six weekdays, for the sake of the Shechinah, and wrap himself in the mitzvah of tzitzis like a poor person.”

paragraphs.text: Tanya, Likkutei Amarim 15: ‘This explains the verse, “You shall return and discern between the righteous and the wicked, between one who serves God and one who has not served Him.” The difference between “one who serves God” and a righteous person is that “serves” is in the present tense: he is in the midst of the service, which is the war against the evil inclination, to overcome it and expel it from the “small city,” so that it will not clothe itself in the bodily organs. Constantly fighting it is truly great work and toil; this describes the intermediate person. … This explains the Talmud’s statement that “one who serves God” is one who reviews his lesson one hundred and one times, whereas “one who has not served Him” reviews it only one hundred times. In their days, it was customary to review each lesson one hundred times, as illustrated there by the donkey drivers who hired themselves out for ten parasangs for one zuz, but for eleven parasangs for two zuz, because the latter exceeded their customary distance. Therefore, the one hundred and first repetition, beyond the habit formed from youth, equals all the others and surpasses them in strength and power, earning the designation “one who serves God.” To change his habitual nature, he must arouse love for God by contemplating His greatness in his mind, to govern the nature in the left chamber, filled with the blood of the animal soul from the kelipah, from which that nature comes. This is complete service for the intermediate person. Alternatively, he may arouse the hidden love in his heart to govern the nature in the left chamber. This too is called service: fighting nature and the inclination by awakening the hidden love in his heart. When he has no struggle at all, however, this love in itself is not called his service.’

All the kings of East and West sleep until the third hour, but I rise at midnight to thank You.” The other says that David spoke before God: “Master of the universe, am I not pious? All the kings of East and West sit in companies displaying their honor, but my hands are soiled with blood, fetal membranes, and placenta to permit a woman to her husband. paragraphs.text: Berachos 4b: A baraita teaches: ‘The Sages made a fence around their words so that a person would not come home from the field in the evening and say: “I shall go home, eat a little, drink a little, sleep a little, and afterward recite Shema and pray,” only to be overcome by sleep and sleep all night. Rather, upon returning from the field in the evening, he enters the synagogue. If accustomed to reading Scripture, he reads; if accustomed to studying Mishnah, he studies. He then recites Shema and prays, eats his bread, and recites the blessing. Whoever transgresses the Sages’ words incurs liability to death.’ Why is liability to death not taught everywhere, but taught here? ... Because sleep may overpower him.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 4a: ‘Did David call himself pious? Is it not written: “Had I not believed that I would see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living”? A teaching in Rabbi Yose’s name asks why “had I not” bears dots. David said before God: “Master of the universe, I trust that You will give a good reward to the righteous in the future, but I do not know whether I have a share among them.” He feared that sin might cause him to lose it. Similarly, Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi raised a contradiction: It is written, “Behold, I am with you, and I shall guard you wherever you go,” yet it is also written, “Jacob was greatly afraid.” Jacob feared that sin might cause the promise not to be fulfilled.’

paragraphs.text: Tosafos on Shabbos 12b, “Rabbi Natan Says: He Read and Tilted”: ‘Here, and in Makkos regarding Yehudah ben Tabbai, who killed a conspiring witness, and in Yevamos regarding the Torah scroll torn in anger, the Gemara does not ask: “If the Holy One, blessed be He, does not bring a mishap through the animals of the righteous, how much more through the righteous themselves.” Rabbenu Tam says that this objection is raised only concerning the eating of forbidden food, which is particularly disgraceful for a righteous person. Rabbi Yirmiyah’s forgetting and tasting before Havdalah, and the cases in Rosh Hashanah of eating on the day that was Yom Kippur in the West, involved food that was not itself forbidden; only the time was forbidden. In Bereishis Rabbah, Rabbi Yirmiyah sent Rabbi Zeira a basket of figs, and the account concludes that meanwhile the figs were eaten untithed. Concerning that case Rabbi Abba bar Zimna said in Rabbi Eliezer Zeira’s name: “If the earlier generations were angels, we are human beings; if they were human beings, we are donkeys, and not like Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair’s donkey.”’

paragraphs.text: Nedarim 10a: ‘Rabbi Yehudah says: The pious of earlier generations longed to bring a sin offering. Because the Holy One, blessed be He, did not bring a mishap through them, what would they do? They would arise and voluntarily undertake naziriteship for the sake of Heaven, so that they would become obligated to bring a sin offering to Heaven. Rabbi Shimon says: They did not vow to become nazirites. Rather, one who wishes to bring a burnt offering volunteers and brings it; a peace offering, volunteers and brings it; a thanksgiving offering with its four kinds of bread, volunteers and brings it. But they did not voluntarily undertake naziriteship, so that they would not be called sinners, as it says: “He shall atone for him for having sinned against the soul.”’

paragraphs.text: Kesubos 59b, Mishnah: “These are the labors a wife performs for her husband: she grinds, bakes, launders, cooks, nurses her child, makes his bed, and works with wool. If she brought him one maidservant, she does not grind, bake, or launder; two, she does not cook or nurse her child; three, she does not make his bed or work with wool; four, she may sit in an easy chair. Rabbi Eliezer says: Even if she brought him a hundred maidservants, he may compel her to work with wool, because idleness leads to sexual immorality. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: Even one who imposes a vow on his wife that she may not perform work must divorce her and pay her marriage settlement, because idleness leads to mental derangement.”

paragraphs.text: Berachos 4b, joining redemption to the evening prayer: ‘The Master said: He recites Shema and prays. This supports Rabbi Yochanan, who said: “Who merits the World to Come? One who joins the blessing of redemption to the evening prayer.” Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says: “The prayers were instituted in the middle,” between the morning and evening readings of Shema. What is their disagreement? It may concern Scripture, or reasoning. As to reasoning: Rabbi Yochanan holds that redemption also began in the evening, although full redemption came only in the morning. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that, since redemption occurred only in the morning, the evening was not a full redemption. Alternatively, their disagreement concerns Scripture. Both expounded one verse: “When you lie down and when you rise.” Rabbi Yochanan holds that lying down is compared to rising: just as at rising one recites Shema and then prays, so at lying down one recites Shema and then prays. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that lying down is compared to rising: just as at rising Shema is recited near one’s bed, so at lying down Shema is recited near one’s bed. Mar, son of Ravina, objected: In the evening one recites two blessings before Shema and two after it. If you say that one must join redemption to prayer, he does not join them, for he must say “Lay us down”! They answered: Since the Rabbis instituted “Lay us down,” it is regarded as an extended redemption. Otherwise, how could he join them in the morning? Rabbi Yochanan said that at the beginning he says “Lord, open my lips,” and at the end “May the words of my mouth be acceptable.” Rather, since the Rabbis instituted “Lord, open my lips,” it is regarded as an extended prayer; likewise, since the Rabbis instituted “Lay us down,” it is regarded as an extended redemption.’

paragraphs.text: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Bo 5 (parallel discussion): On the order of revelation and purification: ‘The statute of Passover corresponds to the utterance “I am the Lord your God,” which includes all positive commandments; the statute of the red heifer corresponds to “You shall have no other gods,” which includes all negative commandments. In truth, reason would require that a person could not attain the preciousness of the utterance “I am the Lord your God” before his heart had been purified through “You shall have no other gods,” for a person must first turn away from evil and afterward do good. But God, in His abundant mercy, placed the utterance “I am” before “You shall have no other gods.” Otherwise, no person in the world could attain the utterance “I am,” for who is the person who can say that he has purified his heart regarding all the negative commandments?’

paragraphs.text: Sefer HaChinuch 430:3 (parallel wording): On the meaning of blessings: ‘The blessing we utter before Him is only a reminder, to awaken our souls through the words of our mouths, that He is the Blessed One, and “blessed” encompasses all good things. Through this good awakening of our souls and the concentration of our thought in acknowledging to Him that all good things are contained in Him, and that He is their King, sending them to whomever He wishes, we merit through this good act to draw His blessings upon us. After this remembrance and acknowledgment before Him, we ask Him for what we need: knowledge, forgiveness for our sins, healing, wealth, or anything else. Likewise, after making our request, we again acknowledge to Him that it will come to us from Him. This is the opening and closing of the blessings, lest we be regarded as a servant who received a portion from his master and departs without permission, as though slipping away.’

paragraphs.text: Menachos 65a, Mishnah concerning harvesting the omer: ‘How did they perform it? The court’s emissaries went out on the eve of the festival and tied the grain into bundles while it was still attached to the ground, so that it would be easy to reap. All the neighboring towns gathered there, so that it would be reaped with great publicity. Once it grew dark, he asked them: “Has the sun set?” They answered: “Yes.” Again: “Has the sun set?” “Yes.” “Is this the sickle?” “Yes.” Again: “Is this the sickle?” “Yes.” “Is this the basket?” “Yes.” Again: “Is this the basket?” “Yes.” On Shabbos he asked: “Is this Shabbos?” They answered: “Yes.” Again: “Is this Shabbos?” “Yes.” “Shall I reap?” They answered: “Reap.” Again: “Shall I reap?” “Reap.” He asked each question three times, and they answered: “Yes, yes, yes.” Why all this? Because of the Boethusians, who said that the omer should not be reaped on the night following the festival.’

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 104a: The Sages told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: Children came to the study hall today and said things unlike anything said even in the days of Yehoshua ben Nun. Alef and beis mean: learn understanding. Gimmel and dalet mean: bestow kindness upon the poor. Why does the leg of the gimmel extend toward the dalet? Because the way of one who performs kindness is to run after the poor. Why does the leg of the dalet extend toward the gimmel? So that the poor person makes himself available to the giver. Why does the dalet turn its face away from the gimmel? So that the giver gives discreetly, without embarrassing the poor person.

So that the giver gives discreetly, without embarrassing the poor person.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 118a-118b: Rabbi Shimon of Shiloh expounded: When the wicked Nevuchadnetzar cast Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah into the fiery furnace, Yurkami, the angel appointed over hail, stood before the Holy One and said: Master of the world, I will descend, cool the furnace, and save these righteous men from the fiery furnace. paragraphs.text: Shabbos 55a: Rabbi Acha bar Rabbi Chanina said: Never did a favorable decree leave the mouth of the Holy One and then turn into an adverse decree, except in this matter. God told Gabriel: Go and mark a tav in ink on the foreheads of the righteous, so that the angels of destruction will have no power over them, and a tav in blood on the foreheads of the wicked, so that the angels of destruction will have power over them. The Attribute of Justice said: Master of the world, how do these differ from those? He said: These are entirely righteous and those entirely wicked. It replied: They could have protested but did not protest. He said: It is revealed and known before Me that, had they protested, their protest would not have been accepted. It replied: If it was revealed before You, was it revealed to them? The ensuing judgment began with those who had fulfilled the Torah. This discussion of the favorable decree and its exceptional reversal is on 55a; the body cites 56a.

paragraphs.text: Eduyos 8:7: Rabbi Shimon says that Elijah comes to resolve disputes. The Sages say: He comes neither to exclude nor to include, but to make peace in the world, as it is said: "Behold, I am sending you Elijah the prophet," and "He will turn the hearts of fathers toward their children and the hearts of children toward their fathers." paragraphs.text: Temurah 28b: The teaching expounds the restrictions in "from the animals, from the cattle, and from the flock." "From the animals" excludes an animal that had intercourse with a person, or with which a person had intercourse. "From the cattle" excludes an animal that was worshipped. The Gemara explains why the exclusions are assigned this way: regarding animals Scripture says, "A man who gives his emission to an animal," and regarding cattle, "They exchanged their glory for the likeness of an ox that eats grass." "From the flock" excludes an animal set aside for idolatry, and the additional "and from the flock" excludes an animal that gored and killed a person. Rabbi Shimon explains that both the sexual offender and the goring animal must be mentioned, because each has a legal severity that the other does not.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Mishlei 9, on Proverbs 9:2 (Sefaria 9:1): Rabbi Akiva was imprisoned, and his disciple Rabbi Yehoshua the miller attended him. Elijah came to the disciple and said: I am a kohen, and I have come to tell you that Rabbi Akiva has died in prison. They immediately went to the prison and found its gate open, the prison governor asleep, and all the prisoners asleep. They laid Rabbi Akiva on a bed and brought him out. Elijah took him upon his shoulders. Rabbi Yehoshua said: My master, did you not tell me that you are Elijah, a kohen, and a kohen is forbidden to become impure through a dead person? He replied: Enough, my son Rabbi Yehoshua! Heaven forbid: there is no impurity in righteous people, nor in their disciples. They carried him all night until they reached a burial cave. After they placed him there and left, the cave closed. Elijah praised the righteous and those who labor in Torah, for whom a place in Gan Eden is kept for the future. Tosafos on Yevamos 61a, s.v. 'From contact and carrying': Rabbi Yitzchak says that the halachah does not follow Rabbi Shimon, and kohanim must be careful concerning gentile graves. Elijah's response to Rabbah bar Avuha was a deflection; his principal reason was that he relied on the majority of burial chambers having a handbreadth of space. He likewise deflected the question when burying Rabbi Akiva: when asked, "Is the master not a kohen?" he replied, "Righteous people do not convey impurity." His principal reason, however, was that Rabbi Akiva was a meis mitzvah, an unattended dead person: he had been executed by the government, and people were afraid to bury him.
