paragraphs.text: Berachos 19b-20a: A teaching asks what the word "and for his sister" adds to the laws of a nazir's impurity. Suppose he was going to slaughter his Pesach offering or to circumcise his son and heard that a relative had died. Might he turn back and become impure? The verse teaches that he must not become impure. Might this mean that, just as he may not become impure for a relative, he may not become impure for a meis mitzvah? "And for his sister" teaches that he may not become impure for his sister, but he does become impure for an unattended dead person. The Gemara asks why this is not barred by "There is no wisdom, understanding, or counsel against the Lord." It answers: This case is different, because Scripture expressly says "and for his sister."

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 104b-105a: Those who interpret Scripture by allusion say that all those enumerated have a share in the World to Come. They expound: "Mine is Gilead" - Ahab, who fell at Ramot Gilead; "and Mine is Manasseh" - Manasseh himself; "Ephraim is the strength of My head" - Jeroboam of Ephraim; "Judah is My lawgiver" - Achitophel, who came from Judah; "Moab is My washbasin" - Gechazi, who was afflicted on account of the washing; "upon Edom I cast My shoe" - Doeg the Edomite. "Over Philistia, shout concerning Me" - the ministering angels said before the Holy One: Master of the world, if David, who killed the Philistine and caused Your children to inherit Gat, comes, what will You do for him? He replied: It is upon Me to make them friends with one another. Bamidbar Rabbah 14:1: Those who interpret Scripture by allusion say that all of them have a share in the World to Come except Balaam. "Upon Edom I cast My shoe" refers to Doeg the Edomite. Israel said before the Holy One: What shall we do? The king of Israel curses them, saying: "Men of bloodshed and deceit shall not live out half their days." The Holy One said: It is upon Me to make them friends with one another. paragraphs.text: Rosh Hashanah 4a: The Mishnah names the first of Nisan as the new year for festivals. The Gemara asks: Are the festivals on the first of Nisan? They begin on the fifteenth of Nisan! Rav Chisda answers: The festival occurring in that month is the beginning of the year for festivals. This affects a person who vows, concerning the prohibition "You shall not delay." It follows Rabbi Shimon, who says that liability for delay requires three festivals in their order, with the Festival of Matzos first. Thus a vow made before Pesach reaches the period after three festivals; before Shavuos, after five; and before Sukkos, after four.

paragraphs.text: Mishneh Torah, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 2:7-8: The different names of the angels express their ranks. They are called chayos hakodesh, which are above all the others; ofanim; erelim; chashmalim; serafim; malachim; elohim; benei elohim; keruvim; and ishim. These ten names correspond to their ten ranks. The highest created rank is that of the beings called chayos, above which is only God; therefore prophecy describes them as beneath the Throne of Glory. The tenth rank is that of the beings called ishim. These are the angels who speak with prophets and appear to them in prophetic visions. They are called ishim because their rank is close to the level of human understanding. All these beings are alive and recognize the Creator; each knows Him according to its rank, but none knows the Creator as He knows Himself.

paragraphs.text: Sukkah 52a: Rabbi Avira, or according to another report Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, expounded: The evil inclination has seven names. The Holy One called it "evil": "The inclination of man's heart is evil from his youth." Moses called it "uncircumcised": "Circumcise the foreskin of your heart." David called it "impure": "Create a pure heart for me, God," implying an impure heart. Solomon called it "enemy": "If your enemy is hungry, feed him bread; if he is thirsty, give him water, for you will heap burning coals on his head, and the Lord will repay you." Read not "repay you," but "bring him into peace with you." Isaiah called it "a stumbling block": "Clear the way; remove the stumbling block from the way of My people." Ezekiel called it "stone": "I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh." Joel called it "the northern one": "I will distance the northern one from you." It was taught: "The northern one" is the evil inclination, hidden and lodged in a person's heart.

paragraphs.text: Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 15: God has set before Israel two paths, one of good and one of evil: the good leads to life and the evil to death. The good has two paths, righteousness and kindness, and Elijah, remembered for good, stands between them. The evil has four entrances. At each entrance stand seven angels, four outside and three within. Those outside are merciful, and those within cruel. When a person comes to enter, the merciful ones meet him: "What have you to do with this fire and these coals? Listen to us and return!" If he does not listen, he says: "In these is my life." They say: "You have entered the first entrance; do not enter the second!" At the second they say: "Why should you be erased from the Torah of your God? Is it not better to be inscribed in it rather than erased? Listen to us and return!" If he refuses, they warn him not to enter the third. At the third they say: "Why should you be called impure rather than pure? Listen to us and return!" If he refuses, they warn him not to enter the fourth. At the fourth they say: "You have entered all these entrances and have not listened and returned. Return even now! The Holy One receives those who return; even now He pardons and forgives sins, saying every day, 'Return, children of man!'" This chapter describes four entrances with seven angels at each, rather than seven chambers. Sotah 10b, parallel concerning seven chambers: The Gemara asks why David said "my son" eight times while mourning Absalom. Seven expressions raised him from the seven chambers of Gehinnom. The Gemara explains that the future harp, with its many strings and greater volume, can also be termed a lyre.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 16a, Mishnah and baraisa: A bridegroom is exempt from the recitation of Shema from the first night until Saturday night, if he has not consummated the marriage. Rabban Gamliel married a woman and recited Shema on the first night. His disciples said to him: Our master, you taught us that a bridegroom is exempt from reciting Shema! He said: I will not listen to you and remove the kingship of Heaven from myself even for one hour. The Sages taught: "When you sit in your house" excludes one engaged in a mitzvah; "when you walk on your way" excludes a bridegroom. Hence they said: One who marries a virgin is exempt, but one who marries a widow is obligated. Kiddushin 2a-2b: The Mishnah states: A woman is betrothed in three ways and regains her independence in two ways. She is betrothed through money, a document, or intercourse. Regarding money, Beis Shammai say: With a dinar or its equivalent; Beis Hillel say: With a perutah or its equivalent. A perutah is one eighth of an Italian issar. She regains her independence through a bill of divorce or her husband's death. A woman awaiting levirate marriage enters it through intercourse and regains her independence through chalitzah or the death of her husband's brother. The Gemara asks why the Mishnah uses the feminine form of "three." It answers: Because it wishes to use "ways," and "way" can be feminine, as it is written, "You shall make known to them the way in which they shall walk." Later it asks: Is the feminine "three" necessary only because of "ways"? Let it say "things" and use the masculine "three"! It answers: Because the Mishnah wishes to teach intercourse, and intercourse is called a "way," as it is written, "The way of a man with a young woman; so is the way of an adulterous woman." Proverbs 30:18-20: "Three things are too wondrous for me, and four I do not understand: the way of an eagle in the heavens, the way of a snake upon a rock, the way of a ship in the heart of the sea, and the way of a man with a young woman. So is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats and wipes her mouth, and says, 'I have done no wrong.'"

paragraphs.text: Berachos 16a-16b, explanation of the exemption: How is the exclusion implied? Rav Pappa said: Like a way - just as a person's ordinary travel is optional, so here the obligation applies to optional activity. The Gemara asks: Does the verse not also concern someone who is traveling to perform a mitzvah, and nevertheless the Merciful One says that he must recite Shema? It answers: If so, Scripture could have said simply "when walking." Why does it say "when you walk"? Learn from this that you are obligated when walking for your own purposes, but exempt when walking for a mitzvah. The Gemara then asks: If so, why distinguish one who marries a virgin? One who marries a widow should also be exempt! It answers: The former is preoccupied, but the latter is not. If preoccupation is the reason, someone whose ship sank at sea should also be exempt. Yet Rabbi Abba bar Zavda said in Rav's name that a mourner is obligated in all the mitzvos of the Torah except tefillin, which are called "splendor." The answer is: There the preoccupation concerns an optional matter; here it concerns a mitzvah. Deuteronomy 6:4-9: "Hear, Israel: the Lord is our God, the Lord is One. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might. These words that I command you today shall be upon your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit in your house, when you walk on the way, when you lie down, and when you rise. You shall bind them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be frontlets between your eyes. You shall write them upon the doorposts of your house and upon your gates."

paragraphs.text: Berachos 16b: The Sages taught: Only three are called Patriarchs, and only four are called Matriarchs. Why are only these called Patriarchs? If it is because we do not know whether we descend from Reuven or from Shimon, then the same should apply to the Matriarchs: we do not know whether we descend from Rachel or from Leah! Rather, up to this point they are sufficiently distinguished; those beyond this point are not sufficiently distinguished for this title.

paragraphs.text: Nedarim 32b: Rabbi Zechariah said in Rabbi Yishmael's name: The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to bring forth the priesthood from Shem, as it is said: "He was a priest to God Most High." Once he placed the blessing of Abraham before the blessing of God, He brought it forth from Abraham instead. For it is said: "He blessed him and said: Blessed is Abram to God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth, and blessed is God Most High." Abraham said to him: Does one place a servant's blessing before his Master's blessing? Immediately He gave the priesthood to Abraham, as it is said: "The Lord said to my lord: Sit at My right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." Afterward it is written: "The Lord has sworn and will not relent: You are a priest forever, on account of the words of Malki-Tzedek" - on account of Malki-Tzedek's utterance. This is the meaning of "He was a priest to God Most High": he was a priest, but his descendants were not priests.

paragraphs.text: Bava Kamma 88a: Mar, son of Ravina, said: Scripture says, "Fathers shall not be put to death on account of sons": people shall not be put to death through the testimony of fathers who have no recognized lineage with their sons. For if the verse meant only that fathers are not put to death through their sons' testimony, Scripture should have written, "Fathers shall not be put to death on account of their sons." Why does it say merely "sons"? Learn from this that people are not put to death through the testimony of fathers who have no recognized lineage with their sons. The Gemara asks: If so, does "Sons shall not be put to death on account of fathers" likewise mean that people are not put to death through the testimony of sons who have no recognized lineage with their fathers? Would a convert then also be disqualified as a witness? They answer: How can these cases be compared? Although a convert has no recognized lineage upward, he has recognized lineage downward. An enslaved person, however, has recognized lineage neither upward nor downward.

paragraphs.text: Bava Kamma 15a: "Free persons and members of the covenant": "free persons" excludes slaves, and "members of the covenant" excludes gentiles. Both exclusions are necessary. Had the Mishnah mentioned only a slave, one might say that he is excluded because he has no recognized lineage, but that a gentile, who has recognized lineage, is not excluded. Had it mentioned only a gentile, one might say that he is excluded because he is not subject to the commandments, but that a slave, who is subject to the commandments, is not excluded. Both are therefore necessary.

paragraphs.text: Yerushalmi Yevamos 2:6: The Mishnah states: One who has a son from any union exempts his father's wife from levirate marriage; the son is liable for striking or cursing his father, and is his son for every purpose, except for a son born to a slave woman or a gentile woman. Rabbi Tanchuma said: This is how Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish answers Rabbi Yochanan: But it is written, "Tziva had fifteen sons and twenty slaves"! Do slaves possess recognized lineage? Scripture came to enumerate Mephibosheth's dependents. Concerning a slave woman, Scripture says: "The woman and her children shall belong to her master." Yerushalmi Kiddushin 3:12: The Mishnah states: Wherever betrothal takes effect and there is no transgression, the child follows the father's status. This applies to the daughter of a priest, a Levite, or an Israelite who marries a priest, a Levite, or an Israelite. Wherever betrothal takes effect but there is a transgression, the child follows the blemished status of the two parents. This applies to a widow married to a High Priest; a divorced woman or a woman who underwent chalitzah married to an ordinary priest; a mamzeres or a Nesinah married to an Israelite; and an Israelite woman married to a mamzer or a Nasin. Where betrothal cannot take effect with him but can take effect with others, the child is a mamzer; this applies to the forbidden unions of the Torah. Where betrothal can take effect neither with him nor with others, the child has the mother's status; this applies to the child of a slave woman or a gentile woman. The Gemara explains the case of a slave woman from the verse: "The woman and her children shall belong to her master."

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 54:2: "Now swear to me here by God that you will not deal falsely with me, with my son, or with my grandson": this is how far a father's compassion extends toward his child. Rabbi Abba said: This is how far the partnership between brothers extends. Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina said: It is written, "My enemies are alive and strong." What He granted Abraham for seven generations, He granted Avimelech for three. Why does Scripture say, "God did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines"? Because his grandson was still alive. "According to the kindness that I have shown you": what kindness had he shown him? He had said to him, "Here, my land is before you." Nevertheless, Abraham did not accept it.

paragraphs.text: Beitzah 3b: A baraisa teaches: An egg laid on Shabbos or on a festival may not be moved, either to cover a utensil or to support the legs of a bed. One may, however, place a utensil over it so that it will not break. An egg whose status is doubtful is forbidden; if it becomes mixed with a thousand other eggs, they are all forbidden. The Gemara asks: If the doubt concerns whether it was laid on the festival or on a weekday, it is an item that will become permitted, and such an item is not nullified even in a thousand. But if the doubt concerns a tereifah egg, it will not become permitted, so why should it not be nullified by a majority? If you say that an egg is important and therefore is not nullified, this is understandable according to the opinion that the Mishnah includes everything customarily counted. But according to the opinion that it includes only things always counted, what can be said? For the Mishnah teaches: One who has bundles of fenugreek from forbidden vineyard mixtures must burn them. If they become mixed with others, and those others with still others, all must be burned, according to Rabbi Meir. The Sages say: They are nullified in a ratio of one to two hundred. Zevachim 74a-74b: Rabbi Yehudah says: The pomegranates of Badan prohibit a mixture in any amount. If one falls into ten thousand, and one from those ten thousand into another ten thousand, they are forbidden. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehudah says in Rabbi Shimon's name: If one falls into ten thousand, they are forbidden; if one from those ten thousand falls among three, and one of those three falls into another place, it is permitted. The Gemara asks: Why specify three, where there is a majority? With two there would also be a majority! The "three" mentioned means two permitted items together with the item that fell among them. Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 110:8: An item that is not nullified because of its importance became mixed with others. One item from that mixture then fell among two other items, and one of those three fell among two further items. These latter items are permitted, since the one from the first mixture was nullified by a majority. But if one item from the first mixture fell among a thousand, they are all forbidden. Nullification by a majority was stated here only to permit the resulting double uncertainty: if an item from the second mixture falls elsewhere, it does not prohibit that mixture. The Rema adds: Nevertheless, one person may not eat all of them. This requirement applies when the original prohibited item is certainly forbidden. If an item of doubtful prohibition became mixed with others, and one item from that mixture fell elsewhere, the second mixture is permitted.

paragraphs.text: Ramban on Exodus 20:8: The quality of "remember" is expressed in a positive commandment; it proceeds from love and belongs to the quality of mercy, for one who performs his master's commandment is beloved by him, and his master has mercy on him. The quality of "guard" is expressed in a negative commandment; it belongs to judgment and proceeds from fear, for one who refrains from doing what is evil in his master's eyes fears him. Therefore a positive commandment is greater than a negative commandment, just as love is greater than fear: one who actively fulfills his master's will with his body and his property is greater than one who refrains from doing what is evil in his eyes. This is why the Sages said that a positive commandment comes and overrides a negative commandment. For this reason, punishment for violating a negative commandment is greater, and judicial penalties such as lashes or death apply to it. Such judicial punishment does not apply to a positive commandment except in the case of rebels who say, "I will not perform the commandments of lulav or tzitzis; I will not make a sukkah": the Sanhedrin would compel such a person until he undertook to fulfill the commandment or until his life departed.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 235b, Raya Mehemna, Pinchas: Binah is in the heart on the left, the side of Gevurah; Chesed is on the right, the water of the wings of the lungs. Chokhmah is there in the brain, and from it comes "a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and streams from Lebanon" - the whiteness of the brain that flows upon the windpipe of the lungs. Afterward the clouds of Binah ascend toward the brain. The secret of this is "Who is this ascending from the wilderness like columns of smoke?" This is the smoke of the altar's arrangement ascending from the heart to the brain, which none of the world's winds can displace. The windpipe, Tiferes, includes six sefirot, the six steps of the throne, which is Imma, the Mother, bringing Chokhmah down to her from the brain to the heart, through which the heart understands. Thus, "Acquire wisdom; acquire understanding": through it Abba, the Father, descends, and through it Abba ascends. It is the ladder upon which two ascend and two descend.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 16b: Rabbi Elazar said: What is meant by the verse, "Thus I shall bless You in my life; in Your name I shall lift my hands"? "Thus I shall bless You in my life" refers to the recitation of Shema; "in Your name I shall lift my hands" refers to prayer. If one does this, Scripture says of him, "My soul shall be satisfied as with fat and richness." Moreover, he inherits two worlds, this world and the World to Come, as it is said: "My mouth shall praise You with joyful lips." Psalms 63:3-6: "Thus I have beheld You in the sanctuary, to see Your strength and Your glory. For Your kindness is better than life; my lips shall praise You. Thus I shall bless You in my life; in Your name I shall lift my hands. My soul shall be satisfied as with fat and richness, and my mouth shall praise You with joyful lips."

paragraphs.text: Shemos Rabbah 47:5: “He ate no bread,” yet he partook of the bread of Torah. “He drank no water,” yet he drank the waters of Torah. He learned Torah by day and reviewed it privately at night. Why did he do so? To teach Israel to labor in Torah by day and by night.Rabbi Yochanan would say to his students: “Come and study Torah during the day.” Nevertheless, Rabbi Yochanan agreed that the song of Torah is only at night, as it is said: “Arise, sing in the night,” and likewise: “She rises while it is still night.” The Rabbis said: By day and by night, as it is said: “He was there with the Lord forty days and forty nights.” Therefore the Sages instituted that teachers of Mishnah should sit in study morning and evening, to fulfill what is said: “This book of Torah shall not depart from your mouth.”Kiddushin 30b: The Sages taught: "You shall place" is read as "a perfect medicine"; Torah is compared to a life-giving medicine. This is like a man who struck his son a severe blow, placed a dressing upon the wound, and said: My son, as long as this dressing remains on your wound, eat and drink whatever you enjoy, and bathe in hot or cold water without fear. If you remove it, the wound will produce sores. So the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: My children, I created the evil inclination, and I created Torah as its remedy. If you engage in Torah, you are not delivered into its hand, as it is said: "If you do well, will there not be uplift?" If you do not engage in Torah, you are delivered into its hand, as it is said: "Sin crouches at the entrance." Moreover, all its activity is directed toward you, as it is said: "Its desire is toward you." But if you wish, you can rule over it, as it is said: "You shall rule over it."

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 108a: A Boethusian asked Rabbi Yehoshua HaGarsi: "From where do we know that tefillin may not be written on the hide of an impure animal?" He answered: "It is written, 'So that the Torah of the Lord shall be in your mouth'—from something permitted in your mouth." "If so, they should not be written on the hides of animals that died without slaughter or were mortally injured!" He answered: "I shall give you a parable. Two people were sentenced to death by the government. The king killed one, and the executioner killed the other. Which is more esteemed? Surely the one whom the king killed." "If so, let those animals be eaten!" He answered: "The Torah said, 'You shall not eat any carcass,' and you say they should be eaten?" The questioner said: "Well spoken."

Two people were sentenced to death by the government. The king killed one, and the executioner killed the other. Which is more esteemed? Surely the one whom the king killed." "If so, let those animals be eaten!" He answered: "The Torah said, 'You shall not eat any carcass,' and you say they should be eaten?" The questioner said: "Well spoken."

paragraphs.text: Chagigah 15a: After Acher went astray, he asked Rabbi Meir: "What is meant by 'God made this also opposite that'?" Rabbi Meir answered: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created, He created with a counterpart: He created mountains and hills, seas and rivers." Acher said: "Rabbi Akiva your teacher did not say this. Rather: He created the righteous and the wicked; He created the Garden of Eden and Gehinnom. Each person has two portions, one in the Garden of Eden and one in Gehinnom. If a righteous person merits it, he takes his portion and his fellow's portion in the Garden of Eden. If a wicked person incurs punishment, he takes his portion and his fellow's portion in Gehinnom." Rav Mesharshiya said: "What verse supports this? Of the righteous it is written, 'Therefore in their land they shall inherit a double portion'; of the wicked it is written, 'Shatter them with a double shattering.'"

paragraphs.text: Yevamos 6a: The Gemara asks: Since we hold that a positive commandment comes and overrides a negative commandment, let us learn from here that it should not override it! If you say that the prohibitions of Shabbos are different because they are more severe, the tanna states a rule elsewhere without raising that objection. A baraisa teaches: If a father told his son, "Become impure," or said, "Do not return a lost object," might the son obey him? Scripture says: "Each of you shall fear his mother and father, and you shall observe My Shabbosos"—all of you are obligated in My honor. The Gemara answers that these cases can be distinguished because they concern preparation for a mitzvah. It also cites a baraisa: Might building the Temple override Shabbos? Scripture says: "You shall observe My Shabbosos and fear My Sanctuary"—all of you are obligated in My honor.

paragraphs.text: Chullin 83a: The Mishnah teaches: "The 'one day' stated regarding an animal and its offspring means that the day follows the night. Rabbi Shimon ben Zoma expounded this: 'One day' is stated in the account of Creation, and 'one day' is stated regarding an animal and its offspring. Just as the 'one day' stated in Creation means that the day follows the night, so the 'one day' stated regarding an animal and its offspring means that the day follows the night." The Sages taught: "Rabbi Shimon ben Zoma expounded this because the entire surrounding passage speaks only of sacrificial offerings, and with sacrificial offerings the night follows the day. Might this law follow the same rule? 'One day' is stated here, and 'one day' is stated in the account of Creation. Just as the 'one day' stated in Creation means that the day follows the night, so the day stated regarding an animal and its offspring means that the day follows the night."

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 65a: Rav Yehudah said: "Night was created only for sleep." Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: "Moonlight was created only for study." They said to Rabbi Zeira: "Your teachings are sharp!" He answered: "They are from the daytime." Rav Chisda's daughter said to him: "Does the master not need to sleep a little?" He answered: "Soon the days that are long and short will come, and we shall sleep much." Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: "We are daytime laborers." Rav Acha bar Yaakov would borrow and repay. Rashi on Eruvin 65a: "The days that are long": the days when one is in the grave, long for sleeping and short for engaging in Torah and mitzvos. "He would borrow and repay": he fixed a quota of a certain number of chapters to study each day, and ordinarily studied by day. Sometimes he was occupied with earning his livelihood during the day, and he repaid his fixed study time at night.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 16:5: "And He placed him": He gave him the commandment of Shabbos, as it is said, "He rested on the seventh day." "To work it": "Six days you shall labor." "To guard it": "Guard the day of Shabbos to sanctify it." Another interpretation: "To work it and to guard it" refers to the offerings, as it is said, "You shall serve God," and, "You shall take care to offer to Me at its appointed time." Zohar I 27a, Bereshit: "The Lord God took the man and placed him in the Garden of Eden." From where did He take him? He took him from the four elements, of which it is said, "From there it divides and becomes four heads." He separated him from them and placed him in the Garden of Eden. In the same way, the Holy One, blessed be He, acts toward a person created from the four elements. When he returns in repentance and engages in Torah, the Holy One takes him from there. His soul is separated from their desires, and he is placed in God's garden, which is the Shechinah: "to work it" through positive commandments, and "to guard it" through negative commandments. If he merits guarding it, he becomes head over the four elements, and becomes a river through which they are watered, rather than through another hand. They recognize him as their master and ruler.

paragraphs.text: Avodah Zarah 3a: The nations say before God: "Master of the world, give us the Torah from the beginning, and we shall perform it." The Holy One, blessed be He, answers: "Fools of the world! One who labored on Shabbos eve will eat on Shabbos. From where will one who did not labor on Shabbos eve eat on Shabbos? Nevertheless, I have an easy commandment called sukkah; go and perform it." The Gemara asks: Can this be said? Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: What is meant by "which I command you today"? Today is for performing them, and not tomorrow for performing them; today is for performing them, and not today for receiving their reward. The answer is that the Holy One does not deal oppressively with His creatures.

paragraphs.text: Taanis 23a: Rabbi Yochanan said: All his days, that righteous man was troubled by the verse, "A song of ascents: When the Lord brought back Zion's captives, we were like dreamers." He said: "Is there someone who sleeps for seventy years in a dream?" One day he was walking along the road and saw a man planting a carob tree. He asked: "How many years until it bears fruit?" The man answered: "Seventy years." He asked: "Are you certain you will live seventy years?" The man answered: "I found a world with carob trees. Just as my fathers planted for me, I plant for my children." Honi sat down to eat bread, became sleepy, and fell asleep. A rocky formation enclosed him and hid him from sight, and he slept for seventy years. When he arose, he saw a man gathering fruit from the tree. He asked: "Are you the one who planted it?" The man answered: "I am his grandson." Honi said: "It follows that I slept for seventy years." He saw that his donkey had given birth to herds upon herds.

paragraphs.text: Makkos 23b–24a: Rabbi Simlai expounded: "Six hundred and thirteen commandments were stated to Moses: three hundred and sixty-five prohibitions, corresponding to the days of the solar year, and two hundred and forty-eight positive commandments, corresponding to a person's limbs." Rav Hamnuna said: "What verse teaches this? 'Moses commanded us the Torah, an inheritance.' The numerical value of 'Torah' is six hundred and eleven; 'I am' and 'You shall have no other gods' we heard directly from the Almighty." ... Micah came and established them upon three, as it is written: "He has told you, man, what is good and what the Lord requires of you: only to do justice, love kindness, and walk modestly with your God." "To do justice" is judgment; "to love kindness" is performing acts of kindness; "to walk modestly" is accompanying the dead and bringing a bride to her wedding. Is this not an argument from the lesser to the greater? If the Torah says "walk modestly" concerning things not ordinarily done privately, how much more so concerning things ordinarily done privately! Isaiah returned and established them upon two, as it is said: "Thus says the Lord: Keep justice and do righteousness." Amos came and established them upon one, as it is said: "Thus says the Lord to the house of Israel: Seek Me and live." Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objected: "Perhaps this means: Seek Me through the entire Torah!" Rather, Habakkuk came and established them upon one, as it is said: "The righteous shall live by his faith." Behold, his soul is swollen with pride and is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith."

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 2:2: What is the path to loving and fearing Him? When a person contemplates His great and wondrous deeds and creations, and sees in them His incomparable and limitless wisdom, he immediately loves, praises, and glorifies Him, and greatly yearns to know His great name, as David said: "My soul thirsts for God, for the living God." When he considers these same matters, he immediately recoils, becomes afraid, and realizes that he is a small, lowly, obscure creature, standing with his slight and limited understanding before the One whose knowledge is perfect. As David said: "When I see Your heavens, the work of Your fingers," "What is man that You remember him?" In accordance with these matters, I will explain broad principles concerning the works of the Master of the worlds, so that they may serve as an opening for an understanding person to love God. As the Sages said concerning love: "Through this, you come to recognize the One who spoke and the world came into being."

paragraphs.text: Yoma 39a: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: "A transgression dulls a person's heart, as it is said: 'Do not become impure through them, and you will become impure through them.' The Sages taught: "'Sanctify yourselves and be holy': If a person sanctifies himself a little, they sanctify him greatly; if he sanctifies himself below, they sanctify him from above; if he sanctifies himself in this world, they sanctify him for the World to Come."

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Berachos 11:2–3: For every positive commandment between a person and God, whether it is an obligatory commandment or one that is not obligatory, one recites a blessing before performing it. Likewise, for all commandments instituted by the Sages, whether an obligation instituted by them, such as reading the Megillah, lighting a Shabbos lamp, or lighting a Chanukah lamp, or a commandment that is not obligatory, such as an eruv or washing the hands, one blesses before performing it: "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to perform it." Where did He command us in the Torah? It is written there: "What they tell you, you shall do." The meaning and arrangement of the words is thus: "Who has sanctified us with His commandments," in which He commanded us to listen to those who commanded us to light the Chanukah lamp or read the Megillah. The same applies to all other commandments instituted by the Sages.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Berachos 1:1–2: From when may one recite Shema in the evening? From the time the kohanim enter to eat their terumah until the end of the first watch: these are Rabbi Eliezer's words. The Sages say: Until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says: Until dawn rises. It happened that his sons returned from a feast and said to him: "We have not recited Shema." He told them: "If dawn has not risen, you are obligated to recite it." This applies not only here: whenever the Sages said "until midnight," the mitzvah extends until dawn rises. Burning sacrificial fats and limbs may be performed until dawn rises, and all offerings eaten for one day may be eaten until dawn rises. Why, then, did the Sages say "until midnight"? To distance a person from transgression. From when may one recite Shema in the morning? From when one can distinguish between techeles and white. Rabbi Eliezer says: Between techeles and leek-green; one completes it by sunrise. Rabbi Yehoshua says: Until three hours, for it is the way of kings' sons to rise at three hours. One who recites it thereafter has not lost the reward of one who reads the Torah. Rashi on Berachos 2a, “Until dawn rises”: "For the entire night is called the time of lying down."

paragraphs.text: Berachos 12a: Rabbah bar Chinena the Elder said in Rav's name: "Anyone who has not said 'True and established' in the morning and 'True and faithful' in the evening has not fulfilled his obligation, as it is said: 'To declare Your lovingkindness in the morning and Your faithfulness at night.'" Rashi on Berachos 12a: "Anyone": One who did not say the blessing "True and established" as it was instituted, and likewise "True and faithful" in the evening, has not fulfilled his obligation. "As it is said: To declare Your lovingkindness in the morning": The whole blessing "True and established" concerns the kindness He did for our ancestors: He brought them out of Egypt, split the sea for them, and brought them across. The blessing "True and faithful" also speaks of future events: we await His fulfillment of His promise and faithfulness to redeem us from the hands of kings and tyrants, preserve our lives, and lead us upon the heights of our enemies—all those miracles that occur regularly and continually.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 69b: Rav Huna said: "One who was traveling on the road or in the wilderness and does not know when Shabbos occurs counts six days and observes one day." Chiya bar Rav says: "He observes one day and counts six." In what do they disagree? One holds that the order follows the world's creation; the other holds that it follows Adam's first days. An objection was raised: "One who was traveling on the road and does not know when Shabbos occurs observes one day for six." Does this not mean that he counts six days and observes one? No: he observes one day and counts six. If so, it should have said "observes one day and counts six," rather than "observes one day for six." Moreover, a baraita teaches: "One who was traveling on the road or in the wilderness and does not know when Shabbos occurs counts six days and observes one." This is a refutation of Chiya bar Rav's opinion. Indeed, it is a refutation. Rava said: "Each and every day he does enough work for his livelihood, except for that day." Should he die on that day? He could prepare two days' provisions the day before. But perhaps the previous day was Shabbos! Rather, each and every day he does enough work for his livelihood, even on that day. How, then, is that day distinguished for him? By Kiddush and Havdalah. Rashi on Shabbos 69b: "He counts six": From the day he realizes that he has forgotten, and he observes the seventh. "Like the world's creation": The weekdays were counted first. "Like Adam": He was created on Shabbos eve, and the first day of his count was Shabbos. "By Kiddush and Havdalah": Merely as a remembrance, so that he has one day distinguished from the others and does not forget Shabbos.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 29b: The Sages taught: "If one must study Torah and marry, he should study Torah and afterward marry. If he cannot remain without a wife, he should marry and afterward study Torah." Rav Yehudah said in Shmuel's name: "The halachah is that he marries and afterward studies Torah." Rabbi Yochanan said: "With a millstone around his neck, will he engage in Torah?" They do not disagree: one statement concerns us, and the other concerns them. Rashi on Kiddushin 29b: "One concerns us, and the other them": The people of Babylonia would go to the Land of Israel and study the Mishnayos of the Tannaim there. Since they studied away from home, the household's needs were not their responsibility. A man therefore marries, so that he will be free from improper thoughts, and afterward goes to study Torah. "Them": For the people of the Land of Israel who study in their own place, if a man marries, the household's needs will be his responsibility and will interrupt his study.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 2a: An objection was raised: "Praise Him, all stars of light." This seems to show that "light" denotes night. The Gemara replies: It means, "Praise Him, all the stars that give light." If so, must only the stars that give light praise Him, while those that do not give light need not praise Him? But it is written: "Praise Him, all His hosts!" Rather, this teaches that the light of the stars is also called light. What practical difference does this make? For one who vows not to benefit from light: one who vows not to benefit from light is forbidden to benefit from the light of the stars.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 43b: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah said in Rav's name: "A torch is like two people, and the moon is like three." They asked: Does "a torch is like two" include the person carrying it, or does it mean two besides him? Come and hear: "The moon is like three." If the count includes him, this is understandable. But if it means three besides him, why are four needed? The Master said: "To one person a harmful spirit appears and causes harm; to two it appears but does not cause harm; to three it does not appear at all." Therefore, learn from this that "a torch is like two" includes the person carrying it. Indeed, learn from this.

paragraphs.text: Shaar HaMitzvos, Vaeschanan 19: "But on the other nights of the week it is not fitting to read Scripture, because Scripture is in the world of Asiyah, and the night itself is the aspect of Asiyah; all of this is judgment, and it is not fitting to awaken judgments. All the more so on Shabbos night itself and on Yom Tov. The Gaon Chida likewise writes in Yosef Ometz that this applies all the more so on the holy night of Shabbos. The cited responsum in Rav Pealim writes that Yom Tov is no different from Shabbos in this respect."

Let him know that his Judge is not flesh and blood, but the Master of all deeds, blessed be He, before whom there is neither injustice nor forgetfulness nor favoritism nor acceptance of a bribe. What will he become? Maggots and worms, as it is said: 'How much less man, a maggot, and the son of man, a worm.'"

Rabbi Zeira said: "Learn from this that the air of the Land of Israel makes one wise." Why does the mother's estate remain with her heirs? Abaye said: "Because the inheritance had already been established in that tribe."

paragraphs.text: Joshua 1:8: "This book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth; you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you guard yourself to do everything written in it. For then you will make your way successful, and then you will act wisely." Rashi on Joshua 1:8: "This book of the Torah": The book of Deuteronomy was before him. "You shall meditate on it": You shall reflect on it. Every reference to meditation in Scripture concerns the heart, as you say: "The meditation of my heart before You"; and: "Your heart will meditate on terror." Radak on Joshua 1:8: "It shall not depart": Our Sages disagreed about this verse. Some say it is a command for a person's entire lifetime, even if he knows the whole Torah; others say it is a blessing. It appears that it was a command to Joshua and likewise to every person until he knows the Torah, after which he should study the branches of wisdom. "You shall meditate on it day and night": After saying "It shall not depart," this repeats the matter to strengthen it. Alternatively, "meditate" means meditation of the heart, as in "The meditation of my heart before You, Lord." According to the first interpretation, "day and night" appears to mean that he should meditate on it by day and by night whenever he finds time free from the affairs of his livelihood.

paragraphs.text: Kesubos 105b: Rava said: "What is the reason for the prohibition of bribery? Once a judge accepts a bribe from someone, his mind draws close to that person, and that person becomes like his own self; a person does not see grounds for finding himself guilty. What does the word 'bribe' signify? That they become one." Rav Pappa said: "A person should not judge a case for someone whom he loves or for someone whom he hates. Regarding someone whom he loves, he does not see grounds for finding him guilty; regarding someone whom he hates, he does not see grounds for finding him innocent." Rashi on Kesubos 105b: "What is the reason for bribery?": Why is it forbidden to accept it even to acquit the innocent? "A person does not see grounds for finding himself guilty": His mind does not draw toward the side of liability so as to find himself guilty, even when he intends to judge truthfully. "That they become one": The giver and the recipient become one heart. Deuteronomy 16:19: "You shall not distort justice; you shall not show favoritism, and you shall not take a bribe. For a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and twists the words of the righteous."

paragraphs.text: Avos 1:6: "Yehoshua ben Perachyah and Nittai of Arbel received the tradition from them. Yehoshua ben Perachyah says: Appoint a teacher for yourself, acquire a friend, and judge every person favorably." Avos 1:16: "Rabban Gamliel says: Appoint a teacher for yourself, remove yourself from doubt, and do not frequently tithe by estimation." Rabbeinu Yonah on Avos 1:6: "Acquire a friend": A person needs a good friend for three things. First, for Torah, as it is said: "I have learned much from my teachers, and from my friends more than from my teachers." Second, for mitzvos: Even when his friend is not more pious than he is, and sometimes also acts unlawfully, he commits the transgression when he derives pleasure from it. Yet he does not want his friend to commit it, for he gains no pleasure from that, as the Sages said: "A person does not sin for someone else." Thus both return in repentance, each through his friend. Third, for advice: He should take the friend as a helper in all his affairs, receive good counsel from him, and make him his confidant after entering a covenant with him, so that he will not reveal his secrets to others who might frustrate his plans. ... Concerning this, Shlomo, peace upon him, said: "Plans are frustrated without confidential counsel, but with many counselors they stand."

'Come to Cheshbon' means: Come, let us calculate the reckoning of the world—the loss incurred by a mitzvah against its reward, and the gain from a transgression against its loss. 'Let it be built and established': If you act in this way, you will be built in this world and established in the World to Come."

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 38a: The Sages taught: "Adam was created on Shabbos eve. Why? So that heretics would not say that the Holy One, blessed be He, had a partner in the work of Creation. Another explanation: If a person's mind becomes arrogant, one tells him: A mosquito preceded you in the work of Creation. Another explanation: So that he would enter the mitzvah immediately. Another explanation: So that he would enter the banquet immediately. This is comparable to a mortal king who built a palace and completed it, prepared a banquet, and afterward brought in the guests, as it is said: 'Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars. She has slaughtered her animals, mixed her wine, and also set her table. She has sent her maidens; she calls upon the heights of the city.' 'Wisdom has built her house' refers to the attribute of the Holy One, blessed be He, who created the entire world with wisdom. 'She has hewn her seven pillars' refers to the seven days of Creation. 'She has slaughtered her animals, mixed her wine, and also set her table' refers to the seas, rivers, and all the world's necessities. 'She has sent her maidens; she calls' refers to Adam and Chavah." Rashi on Sanhedrin 38a: "Into the mitzvah": Shabbos. "So that he would enter the banquet immediately": So that he would find everything prepared and eat whatever he wished.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 91b: Antoninus said to Rabbi: "From when is the soul placed in a person—from conception or from the formation of the fetus?" Rabbi said to him: "From formation." Antoninus said to him: "Can a piece of meat remain for three days without salt and not putrefy? Rather, it is from conception." Rabbi said: "Antoninus taught me this, and a verse supports him, as it is said: 'Your care preserved my spirit.'" Antoninus also said to Rabbi: "From when does the evil inclination rule over a person—from formation or from birth?" Rabbi said to him: "From formation." Antoninus said: "If so, he would kick within his mother's womb and emerge! Rather, it is from birth." Rabbi said: "Antoninus taught me this, and a verse supports him, as it is said: 'Sin crouches at the entrance.'"

paragraphs.text: Niddah 30b: The child does not leave the womb until an oath is administered to him, as it is said: "For to Me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear." "To Me every knee shall bow" refers to the day of death, as it is said: "Before Him all who descend to the dust shall kneel." "Every tongue shall swear" refers to the day of birth, as it is said: "Clean of hands and pure of heart, who has not borne his soul in vain and has not sworn deceitfully." What is the oath administered to him? "Be righteous and do not be wicked. Even if the entire world tells you, 'You are righteous,' regard yourself as though wicked. Know that the Holy One, blessed be He, is pure, His servants are pure, and the soul He placed within you is pure. If you preserve it in purity, well and good; otherwise, I will take it from you." The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught a parable of a priest who entrusted consecrated produce to an unlearned person and said to him: "If you preserve it in purity, well and good; otherwise, I will burn it before you."

paragraphs.text: Bamidbar Rabbah 13:2: "I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey": Because Israel poured out their souls to death in exile, as it is written: "Because he poured out his soul to death," and occupied themselves with Torah, which is sweeter than honey, the Holy One will give them wine preserved in its grapes since the six days of Creation, and bathe them in rivers of milk. Another explanation refers to: "On that day the mountains will drip sweet wine and the hills will flow with milk." "Eat, friends": These are Israel, who did the Holy One's will in exile and did not wish to mingle with the nations, but kept His covenant. Another explanation: "Eat, friends": These are those who perform mitzvos. "Drink and become intoxicated, beloved ones": These are the sages of Torah.

paragraphs.text: Taanis 7a: Rabbi Chanina bar Idi said: Why are words of Torah compared to water, as it is written: "Ho, all who are thirsty, go to the water"? Just as water leaves a high place and flows to a low place, so words of Torah endure only in someone whose disposition is humble. Rabbi Oshaya said: Why are words of Torah compared to these three liquids, water, wine, and milk? It is written: "Ho, all who are thirsty, go to the water," and: "Go, buy and eat; go, buy wine and milk without money and without price." Just as these three liquids keep only in the humblest vessels, so words of Torah endure only in someone whose disposition is humble.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 40b: Rabbi Tarfon and the elders were once reclining in the upper chamber of the house of Natzah in Lod. This question was put before them: Is study greater, or is action greater? Rabbi Tarfon answered: Action is greater. Rabbi Akiva answered: Study is greater. They all answered: Study is greater, because study leads to action. A teaching states: Rabbi Yosi says: Study is great, for it preceded the obligation of challah by forty years, terumos and tithes by fifty-four, the sabbatical years by sixty-one, and the jubilee years by one hundred and three. One hundred and three? There were one hundred and four! He holds that the jubilee effects its release at its beginning. Just as study precedes action, so judgment concerning it precedes judgment concerning action, in accordance with Rav Hamnuna. Rav Hamnuna said: A person's judgment begins only with words of Torah, as it is written: "The release of water is the beginning of contention." Just as judgment concerning study precedes that concerning action, so its reward precedes that for action, as it is written: "He gave them the lands of nations, and they inherited the toil of peoples, so that they would keep His statutes and guard His teachings." Rashi on Kiddushin 40b: "Because study leads to action": He thus has both in his possession.

paragraphs.text: Rabbeinu Yonah on Berachos, Rif 6a, first comment: Our master and teacher said that a difficulty still remains. We see that the mitzvah of tzitzis and tefillin applies throughout the day, yet if a person removes his tefillin and puts them on again, he must recite another blessing. Likewise, although the mitzvah of tzitzis applies throughout the day, if he wraps himself in the garment several times during the day, he must bless each time. He received from his teachers that even if it fell from him and he immediately picked it up and wrapped himself in it, he blesses over it, although he did not intend to remove it. Here too, although the mitzvah of reading applies throughout the day, one should seemingly recite the Torah blessing each time. He considered the following answer: The cases are different. When one removes his tefillin or takes off his tzitzis, that performance of the mitzvah has ended. Putting them on again is therefore another performance and requires another blessing. But after reading once, the mitzvah of reading has not ended, for it applies throughout the day. When he reads again, he returns to the same mitzvah and need not bless again. Even when he reads at night, we do not say that the night belongs to another day and requires another blessing. Although in other matters we say that the day follows the night, regarding reading the night follows the day. As Rabbi Yochanan said in the Yerushalmi: "We are hired workers of the day; we borrow during the day and repay at night." That is, a hired worker must not neglect his work throughout the day. Since we are commanded to read throughout the day, we are like workers who must not neglect their reading. The time we neglect it during the day is like a loan, which we repay at night. Thus the night's reading belongs to that same day, and the blessing recited in the morning to cover his daytime study also covers his nighttime study.

paragraphs.text: Avos 1:3: "Antignos of Socho received the tradition from Shimon HaTzaddik. He used to say: Do not be like servants who serve the master on condition of receiving a reward; rather, be like servants who serve the master without the condition of receiving a reward, and let the fear of Heaven be upon you." Rambam on Avos 1:3: A gratuity is a recompense a person receives from someone who owes him no benefit, but gives it as an act of kindness and favor. For example, a person says to his servant, young son, or wife: "Do such-and-such for me, and I will give you one or two dinars." This is the difference between a gratuity and wages: Wages are given as a matter of entitlement. This pious man said that you should not serve God on condition that He benefit you and bestow kindness upon you, expecting recompense and serving Him for its sake. Instead, serve Him as servants who expect neither a benefit nor a gracious reward. He meant that they should serve out of love, as we explained in chapter ten of Sanhedrin. Nevertheless, he did not exempt them from fear. He said: Although you serve out of love, do not abandon fear entirely; "let the fear of Heaven be upon you." For the Torah has already commanded fear, saying: "You shall fear the Lord your God." The Sages said: "Serve out of love; serve out of fear." They said: "One who loves will not forget anything he was commanded to do, and one who fears will not do anything he was warned against doing." Fear has a great role in prohibitions, especially in those known through received revelation.

: "Antignos of Socho received the tradition from Shimon HaTzaddik. He used to say: Do not be like servants who serve the master on condition of receiving a reward; rather, be like servants who serve the master without the condition of receiving a reward, and let the fear of Heaven be upon you."
Rambam on Avos 1:3

: A gratuity is a recompense a person receives from someone who owes him no benefit, but gives it as an act of kindness and favor. For example, a person says to his servant, young son, or wife: "Do such-and-such for me, and I will give you one or two dinars." This is the difference between a gratuity and wages: Wages are given as a matter of entitlement. This pious man said that you should not serve God on condition that He benefit you and bestow kindness upon you, expecting recompense and serving Him for its sake. Instead, serve Him as servants who expect neither a benefit nor a gracious reward. He meant that they should serve out of love, as we explained in chapter ten of Sanhedrin. Nevertheless, he did not exempt them from fear. He said: Although you serve out of love, do not abandon fear entirely; "let the fear of Heaven be upon you." For the Torah has already commanded fear, saying: "You shall fear the Lord your God." The Sages said: "Serve out of love; serve out of fear." They said: "One who loves will not forget anything he was commanded to do, and one who fears will not do anything he was warned against doing." Fear has a great role in prohibitions, especially in those known through received revelation.

paragraphs.text: Psalms 119:164: "Seven times a day I praise You for Your righteous judgments." Yerushalmi Berachos 1:5: "In the morning one recites two blessings before it and one after it; in the evening, two before it and two after it: one long and one short. Where they said to make a blessing long, one may not shorten it; where they said to shorten it, one may not lengthen it. Where they said to conclude with a blessing, one may not omit the conclusion; where they said not to conclude, one may not add a conclusion." Rabbi Simon said in Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman's name: This is based on "You shall meditate upon it day and night," so that the meditation of day and night should be equal. Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Avin said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's name: This is based on "Seven times a day I praise You for Your righteous judgments." Rabbi Nachman said in Rabbi Mani's name: "Anyone who fulfills 'Seven times a day I praise You' is as though he fulfilled 'You shall meditate upon it day and night.'" Tosafot on Berachos 2a, "He recites two blessings before it": "The seven blessings correspond to 'Seven times a day I praise You' [Psalms 119:164]. The blessing 'May our eyes see' is not counted, because the Sages instituted that blessing so that people would wait for their companions in the synagogue. This applied specifically to their synagogues, which stood in the fields, where they were exposed to danger from harmful spirits. But in our synagogues, people need to wait for their companions only at night."

paragraphs.text: Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:2:4: Rabbi Yudan reported in the name of Rabbi Yehudah son of Rabbi Simon, Rabbi Yehudah, and Rabbi Nechemiah. Rabbi Yehudah said: When Israel heard "I am the Lord your God," Torah study was implanted in their hearts. They would learn and not forget. They came to Moses and said: "Moses our teacher, be an intermediary and messenger between us," as it says: "You speak with us, and we will hear," and "Now, why should we die?" What benefit would there be in our destruction? They again began learning and forgetting. They said: "Just as Moses is flesh and blood and passes away, so his teaching passes away." Immediately they returned to Moses and said: "Moses our teacher, if only He would reveal Himself to us a second time! If only He would kiss me with the kisses of His mouth! If only Torah study would be implanted in our hearts as it was before!" He said to them: "This will not happen now, but in the future, as it says: 'I will place My Torah within them and write it upon their hearts.'" Rabbi Nechemiah said: When Israel heard "You shall have no other gods," the evil inclination was uprooted from their hearts. They came to Moses and said: "Moses our teacher, be an intermediary and messenger between us," as it says: "You speak with us, and we will hear," and "Now, why should we die?" What benefit would there be in our destruction? Immediately the evil inclination returned to its place. They returned to Moses and said: "Moses our teacher, if only He would reveal Himself to us a second time! If only He would kiss me with the kisses of His mouth!" He said to them: "This will not happen now, but in the future, as it is written: 'I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh.'"

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 82b, Yisro: "God spoke all these words, saying." Rabbi Yehudah opened: "Who can recount the mighty deeds of the Lord and make all His praise heard?" In how many ways the Torah warns a person not to sin before his Master! In how many ways it gives him counsel not to turn from His paths to the right or to the left! In how many ways it gives him counsel about how to return before his Master so that He will forgive him! For we have learned: "The Torah gives a person six hundred and thirteen kinds of counsel, so that he may be complete with his Master, because his Master wishes to benefit him in this world and in the World to Come, especially in the World to Come. For we have learned that everything through which the Holy One, blessed be He, brings a person to completeness is perfected through those good things that he merits in the World to Come. Why? Because the World to Come belongs to the Holy One, blessed be He."

paragraphs.text: Sefer HaChinukh, commandment 1: “The commandment of being fruitful and multiplying. The portion of Bereishis contains one positive commandment: the commandment of being fruitful and multiplying, as it is said: ‘God blessed them, and God said to them: Be fruitful and multiply.’ Among the roots of this commandment is that the world should be inhabited, for the blessed God desires its habitation, as it is written: ‘He did not create it to be empty; He formed it to be inhabited.’ It is a great commandment, through which all the commandments are maintained in the world, for they were given to human beings, and not to the ministering angels. The laws of this commandment—when a person must engage in it, how many children exempt him from further obligation, which commandments he is exempt from while occupied with it, and its other details—are explained in the sixth chapter of Yevamos and in Berachos. It applies in every place and at every time. A person must endeavor to fulfill it from the time he is fit for it, which is the age the Sages assigned for marrying a wife. This commandment is not imposed upon women. One who neglects it has neglected a positive commandment, and his punishment is very great, because he shows that he does not wish to fulfill God’s desire to populate His world.”

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 34b–35a: “Moreover, from where do we know that women are obligated in positive commandments that are not dependent on time? It is derived from reverence for parents: just as women are obligated in reverence for parents, so women are obligated in every positive commandment that is not dependent on time. But let us derive the rule from Torah study [in which women are exempt]! Torah study and being fruitful and multiplying are two scriptural texts that come as one, and two scriptural texts that come as one do not teach a general rule. According to Rabbi Yochanan ben Berokah, who says that concerning both of them Scripture says, ‘God blessed them: Be fruitful and multiply,’ what can be said? Torah study and redemption of the firstborn son are two scriptural texts that come as one, and two scriptural texts that come as one do not teach a general rule. According to Rabbi Yochanan ben Berokah, let procreation and reverence for parents likewise be two scriptural texts that come as one, which do not teach a general rule! Both are necessary. Had the Merciful One written reverence for parents but not procreation, I would have said: The Merciful One said, ‘Subdue it’; a man, whose way is to conquer, is obligated, but a woman, whose way is not to conquer, is not. Had He written procreation but not reverence for parents, I would have said: A man, who has the ability to carry it out, is obligated, but a woman, who lacks the ability to carry it out, is not; since she lacks that ability, she would not be obligated at all. Both texts are therefore necessary.”

paragraphs.text: Kesubos 5a: “Come and hear, for Bar Kappara taught: A virgin marries on Wednesday and the marriage is consummated on Thursday, because on that day a blessing was pronounced for the fish. A widow marries on Thursday and the marriage is consummated on Friday, because on that day a blessing was pronounced for Adam. The reason is the blessing; we are not concerned about the cooling of his anger. If so, let a widow’s marriage also be consummated on Thursday, because on that day a blessing was pronounced for the fish! The blessing for Adam is preferable to him. Alternatively, the reason is that the Sages took care [for the welfare of the daughters of Israel], as it was taught: Why did they say that a widow marries on Thursday and the marriage is consummated on Friday? If you say it should be consummated on Thursday, he will rise early the next day and go off to his occupation. The Sages took care for the welfare of the daughters of Israel, so that he should rejoice with her for three days: Thursday, Friday, and Shabbos. What difference is there between the reason of the blessing and the reason that the Sages took care? The difference concerns a man without an occupation, or a festival that falls on Friday.”

paragraphs.text: Isaiah 45:18: “For thus says the Lord, Creator of the heavens, who is God, who formed and made the earth and established it: He did not create it to be empty; He formed it to be inhabited. I am the Lord, and there is none else.” Avodah Zarah 5a: “Reish Lakish said: Come, let us give thanks to our ancestors, for had they not sinned, we would not have come into the world, as it is said: ‘I said: You are divine beings, all of you sons of the Most High.’ You corrupted your deeds—‘Indeed, you shall die like Adam.’ Does this mean that, had they not sinned, they would not have had children? But it is written: ‘And you, be fruitful and multiply’! That applied until Sinai. At Sinai too it is written: ‘Go, say to them: Return to your tents’! That was for the joy of marital intimacy. But it is written: ‘So that it may be good for them and for their children’! That refers to those children who were standing at Mount Sinai. But Reish Lakish said: What does ‘This is the book of the generations of Adam’ mean? Did Adam have a book? It teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, showed Adam every generation and its interpreters, every generation and its sages, every generation and its leaders. When he reached Rabbi Akiva’s generation, he rejoiced in his Torah and grieved over his death, saying: ‘How precious to me are Your companions, O God.’ Rabbi Yosei also said: The son of David will not come until all the souls in the treasury of souls are exhausted, as it is said: ‘For the spirit would faint before Me, and the souls that I have made’! Do not say, ‘We would not have come into the world,’ but, ‘We would have been as though we had not come into the world.’ Does this mean that, had they not sinned, they would not have died? But the passages on levirate marriage and inheritance are written in the Torah! They were written conditionally. Can scriptural passages be written conditionally? Yes, for Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: What does ‘There was evening and there was morning, the sixth day’ mean? It teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, stipulated with the works of creation: If Israel accepts the Torah, well and good; if not, I shall return you to emptiness and void. They raised an objection: ‘If only their heart would remain this way’—it is impossible to remove the Angel of Death from them, for the decree has already been issued. Rather, Israel accepted the Torah so that no nation or language would rule over them, as it is said: ‘So that it may be good for them and for their children forever.’ Reish Lakish follows this other tanna, for it was taught: Rabbi Yosei says: Israel accepted the Torah so that the Angel of Death would have no dominion over them, as it is said: ‘I said: You are divine beings, all of you sons of the Most High.’ You corrupted your deeds—‘Indeed, you shall die like Adam.’ According to Rabbi Yosei too, it is written: ‘So that it may be good for them and for their children forever’; there would be benefit, but death would still exist! Rabbi Yosei answers: Since there would be no death, there could be no greater benefit than this.”

paragraphs.text: Genesis 9:1: “God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them: Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth.” Genesis 9:7: “And you, be fruitful and multiply; teem upon the earth and multiply in it.” Rashi on Genesis 9:7: “‘And you, be fruitful and multiply.’ According to its plain meaning, the first statement is a blessing, and here it is a command. According to its midrashic interpretation, it compares one who does not engage in procreation to a shedder of blood.” Sanhedrin 59b: On commandments given to Noah’s descendants and repeated at Sinai, the Gemara asks: “What about being fruitful and multiplying, which was said to Noah’s descendants, as it is written: ‘And you, be fruitful and multiply,’ and was repeated at Sinai: ‘Go, say to them: Return to your tents’—yet it was said to Israel and not to Noah’s descendants! That latter verse comes to teach that a matter prohibited by a formal decision requires another formal decision to permit it. If so, concerning every commandment too, let us say it was repeated for a particular purpose! This is what the rule means: Why would the prohibition itself be repeated?” The permission to return to their tents thus ends the restriction preceding the revelation, rather than repeating the commandment of procreation.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 10a: “What did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? He brought suffering upon Hezekiah and said to Isaiah: Go and visit the sick man. It is said: ‘In those days Hezekiah became mortally ill, and Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet came to him and said to him: Thus says the Lord: Set your house in order, for you shall die and shall not live.’ What does ‘you shall die and shall not live’ mean? ‘You shall die’ in this world, and ‘shall not live’ in the World to Come. Hezekiah said to him: Why so severe a judgment? Isaiah said: Because you did not engage in procreation. Hezekiah said: Because I saw through the holy spirit that unworthy children would descend from me. Isaiah said: Why concern yourself with the Merciful One’s hidden matters? You should do what you were commanded, and let the Holy One, blessed be He, do what is pleasing to Him. Hezekiah said: Now give me your daughter; perhaps my merit and your merit together will bring it about that worthy children descend from me. Isaiah said: The decree against you has already been issued. Hezekiah said: Son of Amoz, finish your prophecy and leave! This is what I received from my grandfather’s house: Even if a sharp sword rests upon a person’s neck, he should not withhold himself from praying for mercy.”

paragraphs.text: Bava Basra 60b: “It was taught: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha said: From the day the Temple was destroyed, it would be fitting for us to decree upon ourselves not to eat meat or drink wine. But a decree is not imposed upon the community unless the majority of the community can bear it. From the day the wicked kingdom spread its rule, imposing evil and harsh decrees upon us, abolishing Torah and commandments among us, and preventing us from entering the celebration of a son’s circumcision—or, according to another version, the celebration of a son’s redemption—it would be fitting for us to decree upon ourselves not to marry a wife or beget children, so that the descendants of our father Abraham would perish of themselves. But leave Israel alone: it is better that they act unwittingly than deliberately.”

paragraphs.text: Berachos 51b: “Ulla visited Rav Nachman’s house. He ate bread, recited Grace after Meals, and gave the cup of blessing to Rav Nachman. Ulla said: Rabbi Yochanan said as follows: The fruit of a woman’s womb is blessed only through the fruit of a man’s body, as it is said: ‘He shall bless the fruit of your body.’ It does not say ‘the fruit of her womb,’ but ‘the fruit of your body.’ It was also taught thus: Rabbi Nassan says: From where do we know that the fruit of a woman’s womb is blessed only through the fruit of a man’s body? paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 29a: “Mishnah: All a father’s duties concerning his son are obligatory upon men, while women are exempt. All a child’s duties toward his father are obligatory upon both men and women. All positive commandments that depend on time are obligatory upon men, while women are exempt. All positive commandments that do not depend on time are obligatory upon both men and women. All prohibitions, whether dependent on time or not dependent on time, are obligatory upon both men and women, except the prohibitions against rounding the corners of the head, destroying the corners of the beard, and becoming ritually impure through the dead.”

paragraphs.text: Kesubos 64a: In its discussion of a woman’s demand for marriage, the Gemara asks: “Why is a widow awaiting levirate marriage different, so that we do not take up her claim? We say to her: Go, you are not commanded [in procreation]. Regarding an engaged woman too, let us say to her: Go, you are not commanded! Rather, the case concerns a woman who comes with a specific claim, saying: I want a staff for my hand and a spade for my burial. A widow awaiting levirate marriage could likewise come with such a claim! Rather, in both cases it is he who makes the demand, and there is no difficulty: one case concerns his demand to perform the release ceremony, and the other his demand to enter levirate marriage. Rabbi Pedas said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: If he demands the release ceremony, we take up his claim; if he demands levirate marriage, we do not take up his claim.” Rashi on Kesubos 64a, ‘A staff for my hand’: “I want to have a son who will hold my hand in my old age, upon whom I can lean, and who will bury me on the day of my death.”

paragraphs.text: Nazir 24b: “‘If the animal was hers, the sin offering is left to die and the burnt offering is offered.’ From where does she have property of her own? Have you not said: Whatever a woman acquires, her husband acquires! Rav Pappa said: She saved it from her allowance for dough. Alternatively: Another person transferred it to her and said, ‘On condition that your husband has no rights in it.’” Tosafos on Kiddushin 23b, ‘Rabbi Elazar says’: “If the husband gives a gift to his wife, she acquires it entirely, and the husband does not consume its produce, as is stated in the chapter ‘The Presumption of Ownership.’ If he gives a gift to his slave, the slave acquires nothing. Furthermore, they are not alike: if others give a slave an ordinary gift, the master acquires both the principal and the produce; but if others give a woman a gift, her husband has only the produce, while the principal is hers. The statement that a woman has no acquisition independently of her husband means that the husband consumes the produce, while the principal belongs to the woman; land is purchased with it, and he consumes its produce.”

paragraphs.text: Ramban on Deuteronomy 29:17: On the warning about a root bearing poison: “He says, ‘Lest there be among you one whose heart turns away today,’ referring to someone already drawn to idolatry who believes in it in his heart this very day; or lest there be among you an evil root that will blossom and grow, and in days to come put forth evil flowers and produce bitterness. This concerns ‘one who is not here with us today,’ for the father is a root and the son is a shoot that grows from his roots. He mentions the root to explain that he can bring future generations under the oath: the root from which they will grow stands before him today and enters this covenant and oath. ‘Bearing poison’ hints that bitterness does not emerge from a sweet root, and that one whose heart is wholly faithful to the glorious God, without any thought of idolatry, will not beget a child who acknowledges it. Do not challenge this from the verse, ‘He begets a violent son’ [Ezekiel 18:10], for the matter is true and contains a great secret that I cannot explain.”

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 22a: “Rav Yehudah said in Rav Asi’s name, in Rav’s name: It is forbidden to count money by the light of a Chanukah lamp. When I said this before Shmuel, he asked me: Does the lamp possess sanctity? Rav Yosef objected: Does blood possess sanctity? Yet it was taught: ‘He shall pour out its blood and cover it’—he must cover it with what he used to pour it out; he may not cover it with his foot, so that mitzvos should not be treated contemptuously. Here too, mitzvos should not be treated contemptuously. They asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: May one use the decorations of a sukkah during all seven days? He answered: They have already said that one may not count money by the light of a Chanukah lamp. Rav Yosef said: Master of Abraham! He makes an explicitly taught ruling depend on one not explicitly taught. The sukkah ruling was taught; the Chanukah ruling was not taught. For it was taught: If one roofed a sukkah properly, adorned it with curtains and decorated sheets, and hung in it nuts, peaches, almonds, pomegranates, bunches of grapes, wreaths of grain, wine, oil, and fine flour, one may not use them until the close of the festival’s final day. If he stipulated about them, everything follows his stipulation. Rather, Rav Yosef said: The father of all of them is blood.”

paragraphs.text: Rambam, Hilchos Talmud Torah 1:2: “Just as a person must teach his son, so he must teach his grandson, as it says, ‘Make them known to your children and your children’s children.’ This does not apply only to his son and grandson: every sage of Israel is commanded to teach all students, even though they are not his children, as it says, ‘You shall teach them diligently to your children.’ The received tradition explains that ‘your children’ means your students, for students are called children, as it says, ‘The sons of the prophets went out.’ Why, then, is there a separate command concerning his son and grandson? To give his son precedence over his grandson, and his grandson precedence over another person’s son.”

paragraphs.text: Niddah 31a: The Sages taught: ‘There are three partners in a person: God, his father, and his mother. His father provides the white substance, from which come bones, sinews, nails, the brain in his head, and the white of the eye. His mother provides the red substance, from which come skin, flesh, hair, and the black of the eye. God gives him spirit, soul, facial features, eyesight, hearing, speech, the ability to walk, understanding, and intelligence. When his time comes to depart this world, God takes His portion and leaves the portions of his father and mother before them.’
