paragraphs.text: Taanis 20a–20b: “The Sages taught: A person should always be pliant like a reed and not hard like a cedar. Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, was once coming from his teacher’s house in Migdal Gedor. He rode on a donkey along the riverbank and was very happy; he had become proud because he had learned much Torah. He encountered an exceedingly ugly person, who said: Peace to you, my rabbi! He did not return the greeting, but said: Worthless fellow, how ugly that man is! Are all the people of your city as ugly as you? The man answered: I do not know. Go and tell the Craftsman who made me: How ugly is this vessel You made! When he realized that he had sinned, he dismounted, prostrated himself before the man, and said: I have wronged you; forgive me! He answered: I will not forgive you until you go to the Craftsman who made me and tell Him: How ugly is this vessel You made! He followed the man until they reached his city. The townspeople came out to greet him, saying: Peace to you, my rabbi, my rabbi, my teacher, my teacher! The man asked: Whom do you call ‘my rabbi’? They answered: The man following you. He said: If this is a rabbi, may there not be many like him in Israel! They asked: Why? He answered: He did such and such to me. They said: Nevertheless, forgive him, for he is a great Torah scholar. He said: For your sake I forgive him, provided that he does not become accustomed to acting this way. Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, immediately entered and taught: A person should always be pliant like a reed and not hard like a cedar. Therefore the reed merited that a quill be taken from it to write a Torah scroll, tefillin, and mezuzos.”

paragraphs.text: Avodah Zarah 28b: “Rav Yehudah permitted treating an eye with medicine on Shabbos. Rav Shmuel bar Yehudah said: Who will heed Yehudah, who desecrates Shabbos? Later his own eye became afflicted, and he sent to ask: Is it permitted or forbidden? He sent back: It is permitted for everyone, but forbidden for you. Is this my own ruling? It is Mar Shmuel’s! A maidservant in Mar Shmuel’s house developed a burning inflammation in her eye on Shabbos. She cried out, but no one attended to her, and her eye burst. The next day Mar Shmuel went out and taught: An eye that has become severely inflamed may be treated with medicine on Shabbos. Why? Because the blood vessels of the eye are connected to the chambers of the heart.”

paragraphs.text: Rif, Responsum 1 (quoted in Torah Lishmah 519): “Question: Why did the Sages say ‘The reading is a mother’ and ‘The written tradition is a mother,’ rather than ‘father’? Why did they say ‘A father principle’ and ‘This established a father principle,’ rather than ‘mother’? Answer: We have heard no explanation of this. Sometimes they use the masculine expression ‘father,’ as in a father principle derived from two verses, or from one verse, or the statement, ‘The father of all of them is blood.’ It may be said that when something is made the principal source from which something else is learned, it is called a father. But when they say, ‘The reading is a mother,’ other matters are not learned from it; it merely identifies what we rely upon, the reading or the written tradition. They call it a mother because the word for ‘reading’ is grammatically feminine, not masculine.”

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 40a: “A good thought is joined to a deed, as it says, ‘Then those who fear the Lord spoke to one another, and the Lord listened and heard; a book of remembrance was written before Him for those who fear the Lord and think of His name.’ What does ‘think of His name’ mean? Rav Asi said: Even if a person intended to perform a mitzvah but circumstances beyond his control prevented him and he did not perform it, Scripture credits him as though he had performed it. The Holy One, blessed be He, does not join an evil thought to a deed, as it says, ‘If I regarded wrongdoing in my heart, the Lord would not hear.’ How, then, do I understand, ‘I am bringing evil upon this people, the fruit of their thoughts’? A thought that produces fruit is joined to a deed; a thought that produces no fruit is not joined to a deed.”

paragraphs.text: Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed III:8: “How wonderfully wise is the simile of King Solomon, in which he compares matter to a faithless wife: for matter is never found without form, and is therefore always like such a wife who is never without a husband, never single; and yet, though being wedded, constantly seeks another man in the place of her husband: she entices and attracts him in every possible manner till he obtains from her what her husband has obtained. The same is the case with matter. Whatever form it has, it is disposed to receive another form; it never leaves off moving and casting off the form which it has in order to receive another. The same takes place when this second form is received.It is therefore clear that all corruption, destruction, or defect comes from matter. Take, e.g., man; his deformities and unnatural shape of limbs; all weakness, interruption, or disorder of his actions, whether innate or not, originate in the transient substance, not in the form. All other living beings likewise die or become ill through the substance of the body and not through its form. Man’s shortcomings and sins are all due to the substance of the body and not to its form; while all his merits are exclusively due to his form. Thus the knowledge of God, the formation of ideas, the mastery of desire and passion, the distinction between that which is to be chosen and that which is to be rejected, all these man owes to his form; but eating, drinking, sexual intercourse, excessive lust, passion, and all vices, have their origin in the substance of his body. Now it was clear that this was the case,—it was impossible, according to the wisdom of God, that substance should exist without form, or any of the forms of the bodies without substance, and it was necessary that the very noble form of man, which is the image and likeness of God, as has been shown by us, should be joined to the substance of dust and darkness, the source of all defect and loss. For these reasons the Creator gave to the form of man power, rule, and dominion over the substance;—the form can subdue the substance, refuse the fulfilment of its desires, and reduce them, as far as possible, to a just and proper measure.”

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Sisa 36: “‘He was there with the Lord forty days and forty nights.’ How did Moshe know when it was day? When the Holy One, blessed be He, taught him Written Torah, he knew that it was day; when He taught him Mishnah and Talmud orally, he knew that it was night. For day and night are alike before the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said: ‘Light dwells with Him,’ and it is written: ‘Even darkness does not darken for You; night shines like day, and darkness is like light.’ How else did he distinguish day from night? When he saw the constellations bowing and prostrating themselves, he knew that it was day; when he saw the sun prostrating itself, he knew that it was night, as it is written: ‘The hosts of heaven bow to You.’”Shemos Rabbah 47:8: “Another explanation: How did Moshe know how many days he had spent? It is written: ‘He was there with the Lord forty days and forty nights.’ From where do we know that there is no night above? It is said: ‘Even darkness does not darken for You; night shines like day, and darkness is like light.’ How, then, did he know? It is said: ‘I stood on the mountain as on the first days,’ and it is also written: ‘I sat on the mountain.’ We must therefore say: When He spoke with him, Moshe stood; when He withdrew from him, Moshe sat and reviewed what he had learned. Thus both ‘I stood on the mountain’ and ‘I sat on the mountain’ are fulfilled. When He spoke with him, he knew that it was day; when He told him, ‘Study your Torah,’ he knew that it was night. David likewise says: ‘Day to day pours forth speech.’”Recanati on the Torah, Yisro 4: “All agree that the Oral Torah signifies judgment, while the Written Torah signifies kindness and mercy. The reason is that the Written Torah does not explicitly set out laws and decrees as the Oral Torah does, for in many places our Sages enacted decrees, and we are obligated to accept them. All agree, too, that the Oral Torah emanates from the Written Torah. Therefore, everywhere in their teachings our Sages seek proof from Scripture. This resembles emanation: The Oral Torah has no support except the Written Torah. It was not given to be written down, so that it would not be established independently of the Written Torah, because of the mystery of the kiss. A person is therefore obligated to study both. When a person studies Written Torah but has not merited to study Oral Torah, he is ‘a whisperer who separates the intimate friend,’ like one who invited the bridegroom to the wedding canopy while the bride remains in her father’s house, dividing one domain into two. True unification is to join them both: Bridegroom and bride turn toward each other and unite in a kiss and embrace, becoming one, their faces toward one another. Then blessing and abundance increase from the source of nothingness into existence; all attributes of judgment cease, and the white countenance, the face of mercy, increases. This is ‘He meditates upon His Torah day and night,’ alluding to the attribute of day and the attribute of night.”Targum to Shir HaShirim 5:10: “Then the congregation of Israel began to relate the praise of the Master of the world, saying: I desire to serve that God who wraps Himself by day in a robe white as snow and engages in the twenty-four books of Torah, Prophets, and Writings. By night He engages in the six orders of Mishnah; the glorious radiance of His face shines like fire from the abundance of wisdom and understanding, for He renews new teachings every day and will reveal them to His people on the great day. His ranks are over myriads of myriads of angels who serve before Him.”Targum to Eichah 2:19: “Arise, congregation of Israel dwelling in exile; engage in Mishnah at night, for the Divine Presence of the Lord rests opposite you, and in words of Torah at the beginning of the dawn. Pour out like water the crookedness of your heart, return in repentance, and pray in the synagogue before the Lord. Raise your hands toward Him in prayer for the lives of your children, who faint from hunger at the head of every street.”

paragraphs.text: Tosafos, Yevamos 22b, ‘He has no son—examine his descendants’: “Although the unqualified terms ‘brother’ and ‘son’ include even a mamzer, as the Gemara asks above, ‘It is obvious that he is his brother,’ here too the exposition ‘He has no son—examine his descendants’ is needed only to prevent us from deriving the law from Yaakov’s sons. The exposition ‘She has no offspring—examine her descendants’ is needed because the unqualified term ‘offspring’ denotes only fit offspring, as the beginning of Kiddushin states: ‘I have only fit offspring; from where do we include invalid offspring?’ With regard to grandchildren, however, the reverse is true: ‘Offspring’ includes even grandchildren, as that passage also indicates when it says that no verse is needed for her offspring’s offspring, since grandchildren are like children. ‘Son,’ however, ordinarily means only the son himself, as the chapter on inheritance in Bava Basra states: ‘I have only a son; from where do we include a son’s son, a son’s daughter, or the son of a son’s daughter?’”

paragraphs.text: Parashas Derachim 7:18, quoting Rabbi Yechiel Bassan: “Know that Rabbi Yechiel Bassan wrote that even one rendered unfit through sin, such as an idolater, is considered invalid offspring and is not called ‘offspring.’ He proved this from the Rambam, who wrote in the first chapter of the laws of yibbum: ‘Even if he had offspring who was a mamzer or an idolater, this exempts his wife from yibbum.’ This implies that a mamzer and an idolater are treated alike.He raised an objection from the third chapter of Nedarim: One who vows, ‘I will not benefit from Avraham’s offspring,’ is forbidden to benefit from Israel but may benefit from the nations. The Gemara asks: ‘But there is Yishmael!’ It answers: ‘For through Yitzchak shall offspring be called yours.’ ‘But there is Esav!’ ‘Through Yitzchak’—not all of Yitzchak. If invalid offspring are not called offspring, why did the Gemara need to resort to verses to exclude Yishmael and Esav from Avraham’s offspring? We have already said that invalid offspring are not called offspring. Even if you say that Yishmael repented, what can you say of Esav, who was an apostate, as Kiddushin states: ‘Esav was different, for he was an apostate Israelite’? All the more so regarding the nations descended from them, about whom we are discussing whether the person who vowed against Avraham’s offspring may benefit: The tents of Seir and Yishmael are certainly wicked and are not called Avraham’s offspring.The rabbi answered that the rule that invalid offspring are not called offspring is not learned from the ordinary meaning of the word ‘offspring.’ Rather, it is learned from the Holy One’s statement to Avraham, ‘For through Yitzchak shall offspring be called yours’—excluding Yishmael and Esav. This establishes a general principle for the entire Torah. He then asked: Why is a verse needed to exclude Esav? Once Yishmael has been excluded, let us derive from him the general principle that invalid offspring are not called offspring, and Esav will likewise be excluded. He answered: From Yishmael alone, I might have said that Yishmael is different because he was the son of a maidservant; alternatively, it was for Sarah’s honor, since she said, ‘The son of this maidservant shall not inherit.’ We would not yet know that he was excluded from the designation ‘offspring’ because of his wickedness. Now that Esav is also excluded, we learn that wickedness prevents a person from being called offspring.He further asked: If one rendered unfit through sin, such as an idolater, is considered invalid offspring, why did the Gemara not say that one who vows against Avraham’s offspring may benefit from an apostate Israelite? He answered that benefit from an Israelite who worships idols is not permitted because he may repent, and it will then emerge retrospectively that he was Avraham’s offspring. The rabbi established that anyone who repents is regarded as though he had been fit from the outset. These are the essential points of his words.”

paragraphs.text: Berachos 7a: “The Master said: A righteous person who prospers is a righteous person who is the son of a righteous person; a righteous person who suffers is a righteous person who is the son of a wicked person. Is that so? It is written, ‘Visiting the fathers’ iniquity upon the children,’ and it is also written, ‘Children shall not be put to death for fathers.’ We set these verses against one another and answer: There is no difficulty. The first applies when the children hold fast to their fathers’ deeds; the second applies when they do not hold fast to their fathers’ deeds. Rather, this is what He told him: A righteous person who prospers is completely righteous; a righteous person who suffers is not completely righteous. A wicked person who prospers is not completely wicked; a wicked person who suffers is completely wicked.”

paragraphs.text: Yevamos 62a: “It was stated: If a man had children while he was a gentile and then converted, Rabbi Yochanan says that he has fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation, while Reish Lakish says that he has not. Rabbi Yochanan says that he has fulfilled it because he did have children. Reish Lakish says that he has not fulfilled it because a convert is regarded as a newborn child.They follow their respective positions in another dispute: If a man had children while he was a gentile and then converted, Rabbi Yochanan says that he has no firstborn for inheritance, because he already had ‘the beginning of his strength.’ Reish Lakish says that he does have a firstborn for inheritance, because a convert is regarded as a newborn child. Both disputes are necessary. Had we been taught only the first, we might have said that Rabbi Yochanan rules that way because gentiles, too, are obligated in procreation, but concerning inheritance, whose laws do not apply to them in the same way, he would agree with Reish Lakish. Had we been taught only the second, we might have said that Reish Lakish rules that way concerning inheritance, but concerning procreation he agrees with Rabbi Yochanan. Both are therefore necessary.Rabbi Yochanan objected to Reish Lakish: ‘At that time, Berodach-baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters’! Reish Lakish answered: While they are gentiles, they have recognized lineage; once they convert, they have no recognized lineage.”

paragraphs.text: Gittin 12a: “‘For if he wishes not to feed him’: Do you learn from this that a master may say to his slave, ‘Work for me, and I will not feed you’? What case are we discussing? He said to him, ‘Let your earnings provide your food.’ In the corresponding case of a wife, he would have said to her, ‘Let your earnings provide your food.’ Why is that not allowed with a wife? The case of a wife is one in which her earnings are insufficient. Let the slave’s case likewise be one in which his earnings are insufficient! A slave who is not worth the bread he eats—what use is he to his master or mistress?Come and hear: A slave who was exiled to a city of refuge need not be fed by his master; moreover, his earnings belong to his master. Does this prove that the master may say, ‘Work for me, and I will not feed you’? The case is one in which he said, ‘Let your earnings provide your food.’ If so, why do his earnings belong to his master? The surplus belongs to him. Is that not obvious? You might have thought: Since the master gives him nothing when he lacks food, he should likewise take nothing when the slave has a surplus. The teaching tells us otherwise. Why mention cities of refuge? This implies that he did not tell her to live on her earnings, for if he did, why must he support her? And since the latter case is one in which he did not say it, the first case must likewise be one in which he did not say it! No: He did say it to the slave, while the wife’s case is one in which her earnings are insufficient. But the latter part states: ‘If he told her, “Let your earnings provide your food,” he is permitted to do so.’ This implies that the first case is one in which he did not say it! This is what it means: If her earnings are sufficient and he told her, ‘Let your earnings provide your food,’ he is permitted to do so. If her earnings are sufficient, what does this teach? Their breaking is their purification.”

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 153a, Raaya Meheimna, Beha’alotcha (14:78–79): “Through the middle pillar, the vessel, which is the woman, unites with her husband after being sanctified on the left and purified in the waters of a mikveh on the right. Concerning Passover vessels they say: Vessels used with cold food are immersed in cold water and become pure. Those souls that come from the side of mercy, who are compassionate and possess grace and kindness, do not need purification in lukewarm water like those of intermediate standing, and certainly not in boiling water. Through the latter, thoroughly wicked people are purified, for they heated themselves in the fire of the evil inclination. Of them it is said: ‘Everything that enters fire,’ because their contamination is great. But completely righteous people are purified in cold water. Of them it is said: Whoever places a space between adjoining letters is cooled in Gehinnom. If the souls are material, resembling earthenware vessels, their breaking is their purification, as it is said: ‘They broke and became pure.’ The mystery of the matter is: ‘The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit.’ But those who labor in Written Torah and Oral Torah, which are fire and water, and those who labor in the mysteries of Torah, which is light—as it is written, ‘And Torah is light’—are purified through Torah.”

paragraphs.text: Kesubos 111b: “Rabbi Elazar said: The unlearned do not come to life, as it is said: ‘The dead shall not live.’ It was likewise taught: ‘The dead shall not live’—could this refer to everyone? Scripture therefore says: ‘The shades shall not arise’; Scripture speaks of one who slackens in words of Torah. Rabbi Yochanan said to him: Their Master is not pleased that you speak of them this way; that verse concerns one who gives himself over to idolatry. He answered: I expound another verse: ‘For Your dew is a dew of lights, and the earth shall cast out the shades.’ Whoever makes use of the light of Torah is revived by the light of Torah; whoever does not make use of the light of Torah is not revived by the light of Torah. When he saw that Rabbi Yochanan was distressed, he said: Rabbi, I have found a remedy for them in the Torah: ‘You who cleave to the Lord your God are all alive today.’ Is it possible to cleave to the Divine Presence? Is it not written: ‘For the Lord your God is a consuming fire’? Rather, whoever marries his daughter to a Torah scholar, conducts business for Torah scholars, or benefits Torah scholars from his possessions is regarded by Scripture as if he cleaved to the Divine Presence. Similarly, it says: ‘To love the Lord your God and to cleave to Him.’ Can a person cleave to the Divine Presence? Rather, whoever marries his daughter to a Torah scholar, conducts business for Torah scholars, or benefits Torah scholars from his possessions is regarded by Scripture as if he cleaved to the Divine Presence.”

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 15b: “Why did the Rabbis decree impurity upon glass vessels? Rabbi Yochanan said in Reish Lakish’s name: Since their original material is sand, the Rabbis treated them like earthenware vessels. If so, they should have no purification in a mikveh. Why, then, did we learn: ‘These substances interpose on vessels: Pitch and myrrh on glass vessels’? What is the case here? They were punctured, and he dripped lead into them. This follows Rabbi Meir, who says: Everything follows the material that holds it together. For it was taught: Glass vessels that were punctured and into which he dripped lead—Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: Rabbi Meir regards them as susceptible to impurity, while the Sages regard them as pure.”

paragraphs.text: Sefer HaChinukh 173, the reason for purification through water: “Regarding the reason water purifies every impure person, I think, according to the plain meaning, that the purpose is for a person to see himself after immersion as though he were created at that moment, just as the entire world was water before there was a human being in it, as it is written: ‘The spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.’ Through this image, he should take to heart that, just as his body has been renewed, he should also renew his actions for good, improve his deeds, and be exacting in the ways of the blessed God. Therefore the Sages said that purification is not valid in water contained in a vessel, but in flowing water or water collected upon the ground, outside a vessel, so that he may imagine the entire world to be water and himself renewed upon emerging from it, as we have said. If the water is in a vessel, or even passed through a vessel, this idea cannot take shape in the mind of the person immersing. Anything contained in a vessel, a product of human hands, has a boundary. When immersing in a vessel, he therefore will not imagine the entire world as water, as at the beginning, and himself as newly created at that moment. Let one who listens listen, and one who refrains refrain.”Sefer HaChinukh 174, shaving the person afflicted with tzaraas: “The commandment to shave the person afflicted with tzaraas on the seventh day: He is to shave all his hair. This is the second purification, as our Sages said in Negaim, and as it is written: ‘On the seventh day he shall shave all his hair.’ Our Sages said: Three shave, and their shaving is a commandment—the nazirite, the person afflicted with tzaraas, and the Levites. The Levites require shaving like the person afflicted with tzaraas; this took place in the wilderness. Among the roots of the commandment is part of the explanation we gave above concerning water: A person should see himself as though he were created today, as though his hair begins growing today, and should renew his deeds for good. When a person is stripped of all hair, he can be thoroughly cleansed of all dirt. Thus, when emerging from the impurity of his tzaraas, he should perform an act of cleansing upon himself with all his strength, so that he will likewise cleanse his deeds with all his strength and turn them from evil to goodness and propriety.”

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 48:11: “‘I will take a piece of bread, and sustain your heart; afterward you may pass on.’ Rabbi Yitzchak said: In the Torah, the Prophets, and the Writings, we find that bread sustains the heart. This teaches that the evil inclination has no control over angels. This accords with Rabbi Chiya’s opinion, for Rabbi Chiya said: It does not say, ‘Set your heart upon its rampart,’ using the form levavkhem, but libkhem. This teaches that the evil inclination will have no control in the future. ‘For on this account you have passed by your servant’: Rabbi Yehoshua said: From the day the Holy One, blessed be He, created His world, you were destined to come to me. ‘For on this account you have passed by’ is like the expression, ‘So may the Lord be with you.’ ‘They said: Do so, as you have spoken’: They said: Eating and drinking do not apply to us. But you, to whom eating and drinking do apply, shall do so for yourself, as you have spoken. May it be His will that you merit to prepare another feast for the male child who will be born to you.”

paragraphs.text: Yevamos 3b–4a: “The reason is that the Merciful One wrote ‘upon her’; otherwise, I would have said that one may perform levirate marriage with his wife’s sister. Why? Because we say that a positive commandment comes and overrides a negative commandment! We do say that a positive commandment comes and overrides a negative commandment in the case of an ordinary prohibition; but does it override a prohibition carrying kares? Furthermore, from where do we know that it overrides even an ordinary prohibition? For it is written: ‘You shall not wear shaatnez,’ and, ‘You shall make fringes for yourself.’ Rabbi Elazar said: From where do we know that adjacent scriptural passages may be expounded? It is said: ‘They are joined forever and ever, made in truth and uprightness.’”Shabbos 24b–25a, burning sacred food on a festival: “Rav Ashi said: ‘Shabbaton’ is a positive commandment. The festival therefore involves both a positive commandment and a negative commandment, and a positive commandment does not override a negative commandment together with a positive commandment.”Pesachim 59a: “Nothing is delayed until after the afternoon daily offering except incense, the lamps, the Paschal offering, and a person who still requires an atonement offering on the eve of Passover, who immerses a second time and eats his Paschal offering in the evening. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Berokah, says: This applies even to a person who still requires an atonement offering on the other days of the year, who immerses and eats sacred food in the evening. Granted, according to the first tanna: Let the positive commandment of Passover, which carries kares, come and override the positive commandment of completing the day’s offerings, which does not carry kares. But according to Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Berokah, what makes this positive commandment stronger than that positive commandment? Ravina said in Rav Chisda’s name: Here we are dealing with a bird sin-offering, of which only the blood goes upon the altar. Rav Pappa said: Even if you say that it is an animal sin-offering, he brings its sacrificial portions up and leaves them overnight on the top of the altar.”

paragraphs.text: Ran on the Rif, Kiddushin 16a:15, beginning of chapter 2: “Some say: In this case there is also a prohibition … Rather, when Rav Yosef’s statement was said, it was said about the latter clause. From the first clause we do not learn that performing the mitzvah personally is preferable to doing so through an agent, since perhaps its reason is the prohibition, as explained: Anyone who can betroth her himself but betroths her through an agent commits a prohibition, lest she become repulsive to him. But if he saw her beforehand, so that there is no reason for this concern, one could say that he may use his agent even initially. From the latter clause, however, we can learn that performing the mitzvah personally is always preferable to doing so through an agent, since in her case there is no concern that she will see something repulsive in him. Reish Lakish said: ‘It is better to live as two than to live alone.’ This is a proverb that women say about any husband whatsoever: It is better to live as two bodies than to live as a widow, since ‘tan’ means a body and ‘du’ means two. Even so, the Mishnah teaches us that it is preferable for her to perform the mitzvah herself rather than through her agent. Although a woman is not commanded concerning being fruitful and multiplying, she nevertheless has a mitzvah, because she helps her husband fulfill his mitzvah. If you ask: In her case too, there is a prohibition when he gives the betrothal money to her agent without seeing her—indeed there is. However, the Mishnah speaks about her: She becomes betrothed personally or through her agent. Thus, its statement that she acts ‘personally’ teaches us about the mitzvah, since there is no prohibition on her part. The first clause, however, speaks about him, and states that he acts ‘personally’ because of the prohibition.”

Rather, he afflicted himself by abstaining from wine. Hence anyone who fasts is called a sinner.’

paragraphs.text: Taanis 11a–11b: “Shmuel said: Anyone who sits in a fast is called a sinner. He holds like the following tanna, for it was taught: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar Berabbi says: What does Scripture teach by saying, ‘He shall atone for him for having sinned against the soul’? Against which soul did he sin? Rather, he afflicted himself by abstaining from wine. Is this not an a fortiori argument? If one who afflicted himself only by abstaining from wine is called a sinner, how much more one who afflicts himself by abstaining from every single thing! Rabbi Elazar says: He is called holy, as it says, ‘He shall be holy; he shall let the hair of his head grow.’ If one who afflicted himself only by abstaining from one thing is called holy, how much more one who afflicts himself by abstaining from everything! But according to Shmuel, is he not called holy? That refers to letting his hair grow. And according to Rabbi Elazar, is he not called a sinner? That refers to his having made himself impure. Did Rabbi Elazar really say this? Rabbi Elazar said: A person should always regard himself as though a holy one dwelt within his bowels, as it says, ‘A holy one is within you, and I shall not enter a city.’ There is no difficulty: One statement concerns a person who can endure afflicting himself, and the other concerns a person who cannot endure afflicting himself.”

paragraphs.text: Yevamos 61b: “Mishnah: A man should not cease from being fruitful and multiplying unless he has children. Beis Shammai say: Two males. Beis Hillel say: A male and a female, as it says, ‘Male and female He created them.’ Gemara: If he has children, he may cease from being fruitful and multiplying, but he may not cease from having a wife. This supports Rav Nachman’s statement in Shmuel’s name: Even if a man has many children, he may not remain without a wife, as it says, ‘It is not good for the man to be alone.’ Some say: If he has children, he may cease from being fruitful and multiplying and also cease from having a wife. Shall we say that this refutes Rav Nachman’s statement in Shmuel’s name? No: If he has no children, he marries a woman capable of bearing children; if he has children, he marries a woman who cannot bear children. The practical difference concerns selling a Torah scroll for the sake of having children.”

paragraphs.text: Menachos 99b: The Sages taught: Rabbi Yosei says: Even if he removed the old showbread in the morning and arranged the new showbread in the evening, this is of no consequence. How, then, do I fulfill “before Me continually”? The table must not be left overnight without bread.Rabbi Ami said: From Rabbi Yosei’s words we learn that even one who studies only one chapter in the morning and one chapter in the evening fulfills the commandment, “This book of Torah shall not depart from your mouth.” Rabbi Yochanan said in Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai’s name: Even one who recites only Shema in the morning and in the evening fulfills “It shall not depart.” It is forbidden to say this in the presence of the unlearned; Rava said that it is a mitzvah to say it in their presence.Ben Dama, Rabbi Yishmael’s sister’s son, asked Rabbi Yishmael: “Someone like me, who has learned the entire Torah—may I study Greek wisdom?” He recited this verse to him: “This book of Torah shall not depart from your mouth; you shall meditate upon it day and night.” Go and find an hour that belongs neither to the day nor to the night, and study Greek wisdom then.This differs from Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani’s teaching. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in Rabbi Yonassan’s name: This verse is neither an obligation nor a commandment, but a blessing. The Holy One, blessed be He, saw that words of Torah were especially dear to Yehoshua, as it is said: “His attendant Yehoshua son of Nun, a youth, did not depart from within the tent.” The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: “Yehoshua, are words of Torah so dear to you? ‘This book of Torah shall not depart from your mouth.’”

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 65a: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: “The study of halachah requires clarity, like a day when the north wind blows.” Abaye said: “If Mother told me, ‘Serve the kutach,’ I could not study.” Rava said: “If a louse bit me, I could not study.” Mar, Ravina’s son, had seven garments prepared by his mother for the seven days of the week.Rav Yehudah said: “Night was created only for sleep.” Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: “Moonlight was created only for repeating one’s studies.” They said to Rabbi Zeira: “Your teachings are sharp!” He answered: “They are from the daytime.” Rav Chisda’s daughter said to Rav Chisda: “Does the master not need to sleep a little?” He answered: “Soon the days that are long and short will come, and we shall sleep much.” Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: “We are daytime laborers.” Rav Acha bar Yaakov would borrow and repay.Rashi on Eruvin 65a: “The days that are long”: The days when one is in the grave—long for sleeping and short for engaging in Torah and mitzvos. “He would borrow and repay”: He fixed a quota of a certain number of chapters to study each day and ordinarily studied by day. Sometimes he was occupied with earning his livelihood during the day, and he repaid his fixed study time at night.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 63a: Rav Kahana said to Mar, Rav Huna’s son: “But this verse—‘Gird your sword upon your thigh, mighty one, your splendor and your majesty’—is written about words of Torah!” He answered: “A verse does not lose its plain meaning.” Rav Kahana said: “When I was eighteen years old, I had learned the entire Talmud, yet I did not know until now that a verse does not lose its plain meaning.” What does this teach us? paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 104b: “She weeps bitterly in the night”—why these two expressions of weeping? Rabbah said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: One is for the First Temple and one for the Second Temple. “In the night”—because of what happened at night, as it is said: “The entire congregation raised their voices, and the people wept that night.” Rabbah said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: That night was the night of the ninth of Av. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: “You wept without cause; I shall establish weeping for you throughout the generations.”Another explanation of “in the night”: Whoever weeps at night, his voice is heard. Another explanation: Whoever weeps at night, the stars and constellations weep with him. Another explanation: Whoever weeps at night, the one who hears his voice weeps in response. There was a woman, Rabban Gamliel’s neighbor, whose son died, and she would weep for him at night. Rabban Gamliel heard her voice and wept in response, until his eyelashes fell out. The next day his students noticed what had happened to him and moved her away from his neighborhood.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 65:20: Another explanation of “The voice is Jacob’s voice”: Rabbi Berechyah said: When Jacob lowers his voice, Esau’s hands rule, as it is written: “The entire congregation complained,” followed by “Amalek came.” But when he sounds out with his voice, “the hands are Esau’s hands” does not apply: Esau’s hands do not rule.Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said: No philosophers have arisen in the world like Balaam son of Beor and Avnimos the weaver. All the nations gathered before him and asked: “Do you think we can prevail against this nation?” He answered: “Go around their synagogues and houses of study. If you find children there chanting with their voices, you cannot prevail against them. For their father promised them: ‘The voice is Jacob’s voice.’ When Jacob’s voice is present in the synagogues, ‘the hands are Esau’s hands’ does not apply. Otherwise, ‘the hands are Esau’s hands’: You can prevail against them.”

paragraphs.text: Gittin 45a: Rav Nachman's daughters would stir a pot with their bare hands. Rav Ilish found this difficult, for it is written: "One man among a thousand I found, but a woman among all these I did not find." Yet there were Rav Nachman's daughters! An incident occurred and they were taken captive, and he too was taken captive with them.One day a man who knew the language of birds was sitting beside him. A raven came and called to him. Rav Ilish asked: "What is it saying?" The man said: "Ilish, flee! Ilish, flee!" Rav Ilish said: "A raven is a liar; I will not rely on it." Meanwhile a dove came and called. He asked: "What is it saying?" The man said: "Ilish, flee! Ilish, flee!" Rav Ilish said: "The congregation of Israel is compared to a dove. This shows that a miracle is happening for me." He said: "I will go and see whether Rav Nachman's daughters have remained faithful; if so, I will bring them back."He said: "Women discuss all their affairs with one another in the latrine." He heard them saying: "These are men, and the men of Nehardea are men. Let us tell our captors to take us far away from here, so that people will not come, hear of us, and redeem us." He arose and fled, together with that man. A miracle happened for him, and he crossed by ferry; the other man was found and killed. When the daughters returned, Rav Ilish said: "They had been stirring the pot through sorcery."

paragraphs.text: Eichah Rabbah 1:51: Rabbi Yudan said in Rabbi Ivo's name: "His name is Menachem, as it is said: 'For far from me is a comforter [menachem].'" Rabbi Chanina said: "They do not disagree: the numerical value of one name equals the numerical value of the other; Menachem and Tzemach are the same." The following supports Rabbi Yudan's statement in Rabbi Ivo's name.A man was plowing when his ox lowed. An Arab passed by and asked him: "What are you?" He answered: "I am a Jew." The Arab said: "Unyoke your ox and unhitch your plow." He asked: "Why?" The Arab replied: "The Temple of the Jews has been destroyed." He asked: "How do you know?" The Arab replied: "I knew it from the lowing of your ox." While he was speaking with him, the ox lowed again. The Arab said: "Yoke your ox and hitch your plow, for the redeemer of the Jews has been born." He asked: "What is his name?" The Arab replied: "His name is Menachem." "And what is his father's name?" "Chizkiyah." "And where do they live?" "In Birat Arava, in Bethlehem of Judah."The man sold his ox and his plow and began selling felt garments for infants. He went from village to village and from city to city until he reached that place. All the village women came to buy from him, but the child's mother did not buy. He asked her: "Why are you not buying felt garments for your infant?" She said: "My child's fate is hard." He asked: "Why?" She replied: "The Temple was destroyed at his birth." He said: "We trust the Master of the world: just as it was destroyed at his birth, so it will be rebuilt through him. Take some of these felt garments for your infant; after some days I will come to your house and collect payment." She took them and went away.After some days the man said: "I will go and see how that child is doing." He came to her and asked: "How is that child doing?" She said: "Did I not tell you that his fate is hard? Even at his birth there was an ill omen, for from that time winds and whirlwinds came, carried him off, and went away." He said: "Did I not tell you: just as it was destroyed at his birth, so it will be rebuilt through him?"Rabbi Avun said: "Why must I learn from an Arab? Is it not an explicit verse? It is written: 'Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one'; and immediately afterward: 'A shoot shall come forth from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit.'"

paragraphs.text: Responsa Chacham Tzvi 18, reply concerning Rabbi David Nieto's sermon: I see that the words of the distinguished and exalted sage, may his light shine, are the words of the Kuzari, first essay, sections 15 and 16. Its commentator, Rabbi Yehudah Moscato, after many preliminary explanations, writes as follows: "He, blessed be He, is truly called nature, as mentioned there, because He stamps with His seal all the coins of created beings. This is the view of the blessed ones when they say that the Holy One sits and feeds everything from the horns of wild oxen to the eggs of lice," and so forth; see there. Praise is due to the sage who delivered the sermon, may God preserve him: although, as we have heard, he knows the views of the philosophers who speak of nature, he rejected evil and chose the good discernment and holy understanding found in the words of the pious men of our people, of blessed memory, who say that everything is under His providence.I have heard, but I do not understand the complaints of those who challenge him. If their objection is that he says there is no nature encompassing all existence apart from Him, blessed be He, and they consider it a lowering and diminution of the honor of the King of kings, the Holy One, for Him to act without intermediaries, let them know that those who seek the mediation of nature in the governance of the whole are close to falling into a net of many stumbling blocks. Those who believe in God's providence in everything, however, walk securely wherever they turn. If they thought that the sage's words concerned particular natural properties, such as the heat of fire and the moisture of water, and wished to force upon his words the meaning that the thing which heats or moistens is the Deity, this is something of which one should not suspect even a fool or ignoramus among all the unbelievers in the world, much less a wise and discerning man among God's people who believe in God and His holy Torah. All the more so, the preacher's words are clear and explicit, without any need for his defense, that they necessarily concern the governance of the whole. He says: "Rather, the Holy One causes the wind to blow, and He, blessed be He, brings down rains and dews; from this it necessarily follows that the Holy One performs all those activities," and so forth. Only someone perverse and mocking would question this.If they thought it improper to call the acts of God, blessed and exalted be He, by the name "nature," and considered this a diminution of His honor, why did they raise an outcry against the preacher and call after him? The great sage Rabbi Yeshayah HaLevi, of blessed memory, renowned for wisdom and piety, writes at the beginning of his well-known book Shlah, which has been lovingly accepted throughout Israel, in the chapter called Beis Acharon, in the name of the author of Avodas HaKodesh, a great Sephardi rabbi renowned for wisdom and piety whose books have spread throughout the land, that the reward of those who perform God's commandments and the punishment of those who transgress them are natural. All who have eyes and perceive the wisdom of truth agree on this, as that pious rabbi explains at length in his book. There is no need to copy it here; it is available and easy to consult. Likewise, what is familiar on the lips of all the sages of the wisdom of truth, that the desire and will for creation arose because it is the nature of the good to do good, agrees with the preacher's words.These people's complaints are therefore directed against all the sages of the wisdom of truth, the holy ones on high by whose words we live. Yet there is no ground for objection here: the word "nature" as applied to Him, blessed be He, does not have the meaning of a particular natural property that acts necessarily. It means the desire and will of the holy King, for a sound and clear reason. We must therefore be grateful to the distinguished and learned Rabbi David Nieto, may God preserve him, for the sermon he delivered, warning the people against inclining their hearts toward the views of the philosophers who speak of nature, from which many stumbling blocks arise. He enlightened their eyes with the true belief that everything is under His providence. I say to him: May his strength and vigor increase! Whoever questions him after seeing these words of ours, I fear, incurs sin.Although all these matters are clear and simple and require no reinforcement, in order to silence every challenger and claimant I wished to join with me two of the eminent sages of our city, may God protect it. After discussion, the three of us agreed on all the matters stated above, that they are true and righteous. Here in Altona, Friday, the seventeenth of Menachem Av, in the year 5465. Tzvi Ashkenazi, son of the eminent Rabbi Yaakov, of blessed memory.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 5:5: Rabbi Yochanan said: "The Holy One stipulated with the sea that it would split before Israel." Thus it is written: "The sea returned to its strength"—to the condition He had stipulated with it. Rabbi Yirmiyah ben Elazar said: "The Holy One stipulated not only with the sea, but with everything created during the six days of creation." Thus it is written: "I, My hands stretched out the heavens, and all their host I commanded"—from the time My hands stretched out the heavens, I commanded all their host: "I commanded the sea to split before Israel. I commanded the heavens and the earth to be silent before Moshe, as it is said: 'Give ear, heavens, and I will speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth.' I commanded the sun and the moon to stand still before Yehoshua, as it is said: 'Sun, stand still in Gibeon.' I commanded the ravens to sustain Eliyahu, as it is said: 'The ravens brought him bread and meat.' I commanded the fire not to harm Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah. I commanded the lions not to harm Daniel. I commanded the heavens to open at Yechezkel's voice, as it is said: 'The heavens were opened.' I commanded the fish to disgorge Yonah, as it is said: 'The Lord spoke to the fish, and it disgorged Yonah.'"

paragraphs.text: Tosafos on Yevamos 61a, 'Non-Jews are not called adam': This is difficult: at the beginning of Avodah Zarah, 3a, and in the chapter Four Death Penalties, Sanhedrin 59a, we expound that a non-Jew who engages in Torah is like a High Priest, as it is said: "Which the man [ha'adam] shall do and live by them." It does not say "priests, Levites, and Israelites," but "the man." Rashi explains in Sanhedrin that the author of that teaching does not accept Rabbi Shimon's statement here. This is possible according to the texts that read "Rabbi Yirmiyah" there. But according to the texts that read "Rabbi Meir," it is difficult, since we hear Rabbi Meir say in the first chapter of Kerisos, 6b, that one who anoints a non-Jew with the anointing oil is exempt. This appears to be because it is written: "Upon the flesh of adam it shall not be poured," and a non-Jew is not called adam. It is nevertheless possible to say that Rabbi Meir's reason for exemption is that whoever is subject to the prohibition against anointing is subject to the prohibition against being anointed, and whoever is not subject to the prohibition against anointing is not subject to the prohibition against being anointed.Rabbeinu Tam explains that there is a distinction between adam and ha'adam, for non-Jews are included in ha'adam. The statement "It does not say priests, Levites, and Israelites" means that it does not say adam, which would imply priests, Levites, and Israelites, but ha'adam. All the verses cited here use adam; the Gemara does not raise an objection from verses that use ha'adam.Rabbi Meshulam used to say that only in a passage concerning calamity does Scripture use the expression "You are called adam," because it did not wish to write "Israel" explicitly in connection with calamity. But in "ha'adam shall do them and live," it should have written explicitly "priests, Levites, and Israelites," as it usually does. Although non-Jews are also called adam, the Gemara nevertheless objects from the verses cited: since Israel is called adam in connection with calamity, where a passage speaks exclusively of non-Jews it should not call them adam. As for "When adam rose against us" in Psalms 124:2, that expression is used because God had been mentioned; likewise, "You are adam and not God" concerning Hiram, in Ezekiel 28:2. As for "I will give adam in your place" in Isaiah 43:4, we expound in Berachos 62b: "Do not read adam," and so forth. As for "The earth He gave to the sons of adam" in Psalms 115:16, from which we derive in Gittin 47a that a non-Jew has the power to acquire land, it means the sons of the first Adam.

This appears to be because it is written: "Upon the flesh of adam it shall not be poured," and a non-Jew is not called adam. It is nevertheless possible to say that Rabbi Meir's reason for exemption is that whoever is subject to the prohibition against anointing is subject to the prohibition against being anointed, and whoever is not subject to the prohibition against anointing is not subject to the prohibition against being anointed.Rabbeinu Tam explains that there is a distinction between adam and ha'adam, for non-Jews are included in ha'adam. The statement "It does not say priests, Levites, and Israelites" means that it does not say adam, which would imply priests, Levites, and Israelites, but ha'adam. All the verses cited here use adam; the Gemara does not raise an objection from verses that use ha'adam.Rabbi Meshulam used to say that only in a passage concerning calamity does Scripture use the expression "You are called adam," because it did not wish to write "Israel" explicitly in connection with calamity. But in "ha'adam shall do them and live," it should have written explicitly "priests, Levites, and Israelites," as it usually does. Although non-Jews are also called adam, the Gemara nevertheless objects from the verses cited: since Israel is called adam in connection with calamity, where a passage speaks exclusively of non-Jews it should not call them adam. As for "When adam rose against us" in Psalms 124:2, that expression is used because God had been mentioned; likewise, "You are adam and not God" concerning Hiram, in Ezekiel 28:2. As for "I will give adam in your place" in Isaiah 43:4, we expound in Berachos 62b: "Do not read adam," and so forth. As for "The earth He gave to the sons of adam" in Psalms 115:16, from which we derive in Gittin 47a that a non-Jew has the power to acquire land, it means the sons of the first Adam.

paragraphs.text: Avodah Zarah 2b–3a: Immediately the Holy One says to them: "Let them tell us the former matters," as it is said: "Let them tell us the former matters." "Where did you fulfill the seven commandments that you accepted?"How do we know that they did not fulfill them? Rav Yosef taught: "'He stood and measured the earth; He saw and released the nations.' What did He see? He saw that Noah's descendants had accepted seven commandments upon themselves but had not observed them. Since they had not observed them, He arose and released them from them." Have they thereby gained an advantage? If so, we have found a sinner receiving a reward!Mar, Ravina's son, said: "This means that even if they observe them, they do not receive reward for them." Do they not? It was taught in a baraisa that Rabbi Meir used to say: "How do we know that even a non-Jew who engages in Torah is like a High Priest? Scripture says: 'Which the man shall do and live by them.' It does not say 'priests, Levites, and Israelites,' but 'the man.' You learn from this that even a non-Jew who engages in Torah is like a High Priest."Rather, it means that they do not receive reward as one who is commanded and performs, but as one who is not commanded and performs. For Rabbi Chanina said: "One who is commanded and performs is greater than one who is not commanded and performs."

paragraphs.text: Berachos 61a: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda expounded: "What is the meaning of 'The Lord God formed man,' written with two yods? The Holy One created two inclinations: one good inclination and one evil inclination." Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objected: "If so, does an animal, concerning which 'formed' is not written with two yods, have no inclination? Yet we see that it causes harm, bites, and kicks!" Rather, the double spelling is understood as Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi taught: "Woe to me from my Creator, and woe to me from my inclination." Alternatively, it is understood as Rabbi Yirmiyah ben Elazar taught: "The Holy One created the first Adam with two faces, as it is said: 'Behind and before You formed me.'"

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 61:1: "Abraham again took a wife, and her name was Keturah." It is written: "Happy is the man who has not walked," and so forth. "Who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked" refers to the generation of the Dispersion. "Nor stood in the way of sinners" refers to the people of Sodom, as it is said: "The people of Sodom were wicked and sinful." "Nor sat in the seat of scoffers" refers to Avimelech, as it is said: "Behold, my land is before you." "But his delight is in the Torah of the Lord" corresponds to: "For I have known him, so that he will command.""And in his Torah he meditates": Rabbi Shimon said: "His father did not teach him, and he had no teacher. From where, then, did he learn Torah? The Holy One prepared his two kidneys for him like two teachers, and they flowed forth and taught him Torah and wisdom. Thus it is written: 'I will bless the Lord who has counseled me; even at night my kidneys instruct me.'""He shall be like a planted tree": The Holy One planted him in the Land of Israel. "Which yields its fruit in its season" refers to Yishmael. "Its leaf does not wither" refers to Yitzchak. "And whatever he does succeeds" refers to the children of Keturah, as it is said: "Abraham again took a wife."

paragraphs.text: Bava Basra 15b: This is a dispute among Tannaim, for it was taught in a baraisa: Rabbi Elazar says: "Job lived in the days when the judges judged, as it is said: 'Behold, all of you have seen; why, then, do you speak such vanities?' Which generation was entirely vanity? The generation when the judges judged." Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah says: "Job lived in the days of Achashverosh, as it is said: 'Women as beautiful as Job's daughters were not found in all the land.' In which generation were beautiful women sought? The generation of Achashverosh." But perhaps it was in David's days, as it is written: "They sought a beautiful young woman"! There the search was "throughout the territory of Israel"; here it was "in all the land."Rabbi Nathan says: "Job lived in the days of the kingdom of Sheba, as it is said: 'Sheba fell upon them and took them.'" The Sages say: "Job lived in the days of the Chaldeans, as it is said: 'The Chaldeans formed three bands.'" Some say: "Job lived in Jacob's days and married Dinah, Jacob's daughter." Here it is written: "You speak as one of the foolish women speaks"; and there it is written: "For he committed a disgraceful act in Israel."All these Tannaim hold that Job was an Israelite, except for the opinion introduced by "some say." For if you suppose that he was one of the nations, did the Divine Presence rest upon the nations after Moshe died? It was taught that Moshe asked that the Divine Presence should not rest upon the nations, and his request was granted, as it is said: "I and Your people shall be distinguished."

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 2:1: "Israel are precious to Me." In the ordinary course of the world, a thousand people enter the study of Scripture, and a hundred emerge from them. A hundred enter the study of Mishnah, and ten emerge from them. Ten enter the study of Talmud, and one emerges from them. Thus it is written: "One man among a thousand I found."Another explanation: "One man among a thousand I found" refers to Abraham; "but a woman among all these I did not find" refers to Sarah. Another explanation: "One man among a thousand I found" refers to Amram; "but a woman among all these I did not find" refers to Yocheved. Another explanation: "One man among a thousand I found" refers to Moshe; "but a woman among all these I did not find" refers to the women of the generation of the wilderness. Rabbi says: "The women of the generation of the wilderness were upright. Once they heard that they were forbidden to their husbands, they immediately locked their doors." The Holy One said: "Israel are precious to Me."

paragraphs.text: Zohar II, 139b, Terumah 65, parallel passage: He opened and said: "'You shall make the Tabernacle of ten curtains,' and so forth. Here is the mystery of unity, for the arrangement of the Tabernacle consists of many levels. Concerning it, it is written: 'The Tabernacle shall be one,' to show that all the limbs of the body are together the mystery of one body."A person has many limbs, upper and lower: some inward and concealed, and some outward and revealed. All of them are called one body, and the person is called one through their single union. So too the Tabernacle: all its parts follow the pattern above. When everything is joined together as one, then it is written: 'The Tabernacle shall be one.'"The commandments of the Torah are all limbs and organs in the supernal mystery. When all are joined as one, they all ascend to one mystery. The mystery of the Tabernacle, whose parts are limbs and organs, ascends entirely to the mystery of Adam, like the commandments of the Torah. For all the Torah's commandments are in the mystery of Adam, male and female; when they are joined together, they are one, the mystery of Adam. Whoever diminishes even one commandment of the Torah is as though he diminishes the image of faith, for all of them are limbs and organs in the image of Adam. Therefore everything ascends in the mystery of unity."Therefore Israel are one nation, as it is written: 'You are My flock, the flock of My pasture; you are man.' It is also written: 'Who is like Your people, like Israel,' and so forth."

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 48a: Where are these four cubits written in Scripture? It was taught in a baraisa: "'Let each man remain in his place' means a space corresponding to the space beneath him. How much is that space? His body is three cubits, and another cubit allows him to stretch out his hands and feet"; these are Rabbi Meir's words. Rabbi Yehudah says: "His body is three cubits, and another cubit allows him to take an object from beneath his feet and place it beneath his head." What difference is there between them? The difference is whether the four cubits are measured precisely.

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 31b: ‘Rabbi Simon and Rabbi Elazar were sitting when Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha passed. One said to the other: “Let us rise before him, for he fears sin.” The other replied: “Let us rise before him, for he is learned in Torah.” The first answered: “I tell you he fears sin, and you tell me he is learned in Torah?” It may be established that Rabbi Elazar was the one who described him as fearing sin, since Rabbi Yochanan said in Rabbi Elazar’s name: “God has nothing in His world but fear of Heaven, as it is written: ‘Now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, except to fear Him,’ etc.; and, ‘He said to man: Behold, fear of the Lord is wisdom,’ etc. In Greek, ‘one’ is called hen.” This establishes the attribution.’

paragraphs.text: Avos 3:17: Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah says: "If there is no Torah, there is no proper conduct; if there is no proper conduct, there is no Torah. If there is no wisdom, there is no fear; if there is no fear, there is no wisdom. If there is no understanding, there is no knowledge; if there is no knowledge, there is no understanding. If there is no flour, there is no Torah; if there is no Torah, there is no flour." He used to say: "One whose wisdom exceeds his deeds resembles a tree with many branches but few roots. The wind comes, uproots it, and overturns it, as it is said: 'He shall be like a bare tree in the wilderness; he shall not see when good comes, but shall dwell in scorched places in the desert, in a salt land that is uninhabited.' But one whose deeds exceed his wisdom resembles a tree with few branches but many roots. Even if all the winds in the world come and blow upon it, they cannot move it from its place, as it is said: 'He shall be like a tree planted beside water, sending its roots toward a stream. It shall not fear when heat comes; its leaves shall remain green. In a year of drought it shall not worry, nor cease bearing fruit.'"

paragraphs.text: Yoma 72b: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in Rabbi Yonassan's name: "What does 'Why is there a price in a fool's hand to acquire wisdom, when he has no heart?' mean? Woe to the enemies of Torah scholars who study Torah but lack fear of Heaven."Sanhedrin 106b: Rabbi said: "Doeg and Achitophel asked four hundred questions about a tower suspended in the air, and not one was resolved for them." Rava said: "Is posing questions a mark of greatness? In Rav Yehudah's time all their study concerned damages, while we study much of Uktzin. When Rav Yehudah reached the case of a woman pressing vegetables in a pot, or, according to another version, olives pressed with their leaves being pure, he said: 'I see here the intricate arguments of Rav and Shmuel.' We study Uktzin in thirteen academies, yet Rav Yehudah would remove his shoe and rain would come, while we cry out and no one heeds us. Rather, God desires the heart, as it is written: 'The Lord sees the heart.'"Shabbos 31a: Rava said: "When a person is brought to judgment, he is asked: Did you conduct business faithfully? Did you set times for Torah? Did you engage in procreation? Did you anticipate salvation? Did you reason deeply in wisdom? Did you infer one matter from another? Nevertheless, if fear of the Lord is his treasure, yes; if not, no. This may be compared to a man who told his agent: 'Bring a kor of wheat up to the loft for me.' He went and brought it up. The man asked: 'Did you mix a kav of preservative into it for me?' He replied: 'No.' The man said: 'It would have been better had you not brought it up.'"

paragraphs.text: Rema, Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 1:1: "I have set the Lord before me always" is a great principle in Torah and in the qualities of the righteous who walk before God. A person's sitting, movements, and activities when he is alone at home are unlike his sitting, movements, and activities before a great king. His speech and free expression among his household and relatives are unlike his speech in the king's presence. All the more so, when a person takes to heart that the great King, the Holy One, whose glory fills the whole earth, stands over him and sees his deeds, as it is said: "Can a man hide in secret places, and I not see him? says the Lord," fear, submission before God, and constant shame before Him will immediately come upon him. He should not be ashamed before people who mock his service of God. Even in private, and when lying upon his bed, he should know before Whom he lies. Immediately upon waking, he should rise eagerly to serve his Creator.

paragraphs.text: Berachos 10a: Rabbi Yochanan said in Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's name: "What does 'She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the Torah of kindness is upon her tongue' mean? About whom did Solomon say this verse? He said it about his father David, who dwelt in five worlds and sang praise. He dwelt in his mother's womb and sang praise, as it is said: 'Bless the Lord, my soul, and all that is within me, His holy name.' He emerged into the world, gazed at the stars and constellations, and sang praise, as it is said: 'Bless the Lord, His angels, mighty in strength who do His word, listening to the voice of His word; bless the Lord, all His hosts.' He nursed at his mother's breasts, looked at them, and sang praise, as it is said: 'Bless the Lord, my soul, and do not forget all His benefits.'" What are "all His benefits"? Rabbi Abahu said: "He made her breasts in the place of understanding." Why? Rav Yehudah said: "So that the infant should not look at a place of nakedness." Rav Masna said: "So that he should not nurse from a place of filth." David saw the downfall of the wicked and sang praise, as it is said: "Let sinners cease from the earth, and let the wicked be no more. Bless the Lord, my soul; hallelujah." He contemplated the day of death and sang praise, as it is said: "Bless the Lord, my soul. Lord my God, You are very great; You have clothed Yourself in majesty and splendor." How does this refer to the day of death? Rabbah bar Rav Shila said: "From the end of the passage: 'You hide Your face, they are terrified; You gather in their spirit, they expire.'"

paragraphs.text: Yoma 36b: The Sages taught: How does one confess? "I have committed iniquity, rebelled, and sinned." Concerning the scapegoat it says: "He shall confess over it all the iniquities of the children of Israel and all their rebellions, for all their sins." Concerning Moses it says: "Forgiving iniquity, rebellion, and sin." These are Rabbi Meir's words. The Sages say: "Iniquities" are deliberate sins, as it is said: "That person shall surely be cut off; his iniquity is upon him." "Rebellions" are acts of rebellion, as it is said: "The king of Moab has rebelled against me," and, "Then Livnah rebelled at that time." "All their sins" are inadvertent sins, as it is said: "If a person sins inadvertently." After confessing deliberate sins and acts of rebellion, should he go back and confess inadvertent sins? Rather, this is how he confessed: "I have sinned, committed iniquity, and rebelled before You, I and my household." David likewise says: "We have sinned with our fathers; we have committed iniquity and acted wickedly." Solomon likewise says: "We have sinned, acted wickedly, and rebelled." Daniel likewise says: "We have sinned, committed iniquity, acted wickedly, and rebelled." Why, then, did Moses say "Forgiving iniquity, rebellion, and sin"? Moses said before the Holy One: "Master of the world, when Israel sins before You and repents, treat their deliberate sins as inadvertent sins." Rabbah bar Shmuel said in Rav's name: "The halachah follows the Sages." Is that not obvious, since the halachah follows the majority against an individual? One might have thought that Rabbi Meir's reasoning was convincing because Moses' verse supports him; therefore this ruling was needed. A man who led the prayer before Rabbah followed Rabbi Meir's order. Rabbah said to him: "You abandoned the Sages and acted according to Rabbi Meir?" He replied: "I hold like Rabbi Meir, as it is written in the Torah of Moses."

paragraphs.text: Sifra, Bechukotai, Section 2:1-2: "But if you will not listen to Me": if you will not listen to the Sages' interpretation. Could this refer to what is written in the Torah? When it says, "And you will not perform all these commandments," what is written in the Torah has already been stated. What, then, does "If you will not listen" mean? Listening to the Sages' interpretation. "But if you will not listen to Me": what does "to Me" teach? It refers specifically to one who knows his Master and intends to rebel against Him. Likewise it says, "Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter": the words "before the Lord" appear unnecessary, but they teach that he knew his Master and intended to rebel against Him. Likewise it says, "The men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinful against the Lord": the words "against the Lord" appear unnecessary, but they teach that they knew their Master and intended to rebel against Him.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 86a: “Abaye said, as it is taught: ‘You shall love the Lord your God’—cause the name of Heaven to become beloved through you. One should read Scripture, study Mishnah, attend upon Torah scholars, and deal pleasantly with people. What do people say of him? ‘Fortunate is his father who taught him Torah; fortunate is his teacher who taught him Torah! Woe to people who have not learned Torah! See how beautiful are the ways and how proper are the deeds of this person who learned Torah.’ Of him Scripture says: ‘He said to me: You are My servant, Israel, in whom I shall be glorified.’ But of one who reads Scripture, studies Mishnah, and attends upon Torah scholars, yet his dealings are not honest and his speech with people is not pleasant, what do people say? ‘Woe to this person who learned Torah; woe to his father who taught him Torah; woe to his teacher who taught him Torah! See how corrupt are the deeds and how ugly are the ways of this person who learned Torah.’ Of him Scripture says: ‘When they said of them: These are the Lord’s people, yet they have left His land.’”

paragraphs.text: Yevamos 109b: “Anyone who says, ‘I have nothing but Torah,’ has nothing but Torah. This too is obvious! Rather, he does not even have Torah. Why? Rav Pappa said: Scripture says, ‘You shall learn and perform.’ Whoever is included in performing is included in learning; whoever is not included in performing is not included in learning. Alternatively, the statement may remain as you originally explained it: Anyone who says, ‘I have nothing but Torah,’ has nothing but Torah. This is necessary for one who teaches others, and they go and act. You might have thought that he himself receives reward; it therefore teaches us otherwise.”

paragraphs.text: Yoma 72b: “Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: What does ‘This is the Torah that Moses placed’ mean? If he merits, it becomes an elixir of life for him; if he does not merit, it becomes a poison of death for him. This is what Rava said: For one who is skilled in it, it is an elixir of life; for one who is not skilled in it, it is a poison of death. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said: Rabbi Yonassan raised a contradiction: It is written, ‘The Lord’s precepts are upright, gladdening the heart,’ and it is written, ‘The Lord’s word is refined.’ If he merits, it gladdens him; if he does not merit, it refines him. Reish Lakish said: This is derived from the verse itself: If he merits, it refines him for life; if he does not merit, it refines him for death. ‘Fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever.’ Rabbi Chanina said: This refers to one who studies Torah in purity. What does that mean? He marries and afterward studies Torah.”

paragraphs.text: Sotah 5a: “Rabbi Elazar said: Anyone who is arrogant—his dust will not be stirred, as it is said: ‘Awake and sing, dwellers in the dust.’ It does not say ‘those lying in the dust,’ but ‘dwellers in the dust’—one who became a neighbor to the dust during his lifetime. Rabbi Elazar also said: The Divine Presence laments over anyone who is arrogant, as it is said: ‘The lofty He knows from afar.’ Rav Avira, or according to another version Rabbi Elazar, expounded: Come and see how the Holy One’s way differs from the way of flesh and blood. A lofty person sees another lofty person, but does not see the lowly. The Holy One’s way is different: He is lofty and sees the lowly, as it is said: ‘For the Lord is lofty, yet He sees the lowly.’ Rav Chisda, or according to another version Mar Ukva, said: Regarding anyone who is arrogant, the Holy One says: ‘He and I cannot dwell together in the world,’ as it is said: ‘One who secretly slanders his fellow, him I shall cut off; one with haughty eyes and a proud heart, him I cannot bear.’ Read it as: ‘With him I cannot dwell.’ Some teach this concerning those who speak slander. Rabbi Alexandri said: Even a slight wind disturbs anyone who is arrogant, as it is said: ‘The wicked are like the troubled sea.’ If even a slight wind disturbs the sea, which contains so many quarter-log measures, all the more a person, who contains only one such measure [of blood]. Rav Chiya bar Ashi said in Rav’s name: A Torah scholar should possess an eighth of an eighth of pride. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, said: It crowns him like the awns of an ear of grain. Rava said: Under a ban is one who possesses it, and under a ban is one who lacks it. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: Neither it nor any part of it! Is it a small thing that Scripture calls every proud heart an abomination to the Lord?”

paragraphs.text: Berachos 19b: The Gemara considers the scope of human dignity: “Come and hear: Human dignity is so great that it overrides a prohibition in the Torah. Why? Let us say, ‘There is no wisdom, understanding, or counsel against the Lord’! Rav bar Shava explained before Rav Kahana: This concerns the prohibition of ‘You shall not turn aside.’ They laughed at him: Is not ‘You shall not turn aside’ a Torah prohibition? Rav Kahana said: A great man has stated a teaching; do not laugh at him. All rabbinic enactments were based upon the prohibition of ‘You shall not turn aside,’ and for a person’s dignity the Sages permitted a relaxation of their own enactments.”

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 1:1: ‘Rabbi Hoshaya Rabbah opened: “And I was beside Him an amon; and I was His delight day by day” (Proverbs 8:30). Amon means a tutor; amon means covered; amon means hidden; and some say amon means great.… Another interpretation: amon—a craftsman (uman). The Torah says: I was the instrument of craftsmanship of the Holy One, blessed be He. In the way of the world, a king of flesh and blood who builds a palace does not build it from his own knowledge but from the knowledge of a craftsman; and the craftsman does not build it from his own knowledge, but has plans and notebooks to know how to make the rooms and how to make the small doorways. So the Holy One, blessed be He, would look into the Torah and create the world. And the Torah says, “In the beginning (bereishis) God created”—and “beginning” is none other than Torah, as you say, “The Lord acquired me as the beginning of His way” (Proverbs 8:22).’

paragraphs.text: Rashi there explains: ‘Babylonians went to the Land of Israel to study the tannaim’s Mishnah teachings. Since they studied away from home, household needs were not their responsibility. Such a person marries to avoid sexual thoughts and then travels to study Torah. For residents of the Land of Israel who study locally, marriage brings household responsibilities that interrupt their studies.’ Tosafos, on ‘This applies to us, that to them,’ explain: ‘Rabbi Yochanan’s statement, “With a millstone around his neck, will he study Torah?” addresses Babylonians, who cannot leave their wives and go to study, and are also poor. Shmuel’s instruction to marry first addresses residents of the Land of Israel, who can study locally and are also wealthy; it is better for them to marry and study Torah in purity.’

If so, a man of desire will find room to be steeped in lewdness with his wife or his many wives, and to be among the guzzlers of wine and the gluttons of meat, and to speak as he wishes of all vulgarities, since this prohibition is not mentioned in the Torah; and he will be a scoundrel with the license of the Torah. Upon seeing them, Rabbi Chanina went upstairs and prayed. When he came down, he told them: “Go; the fever has left him.” They asked: “Are you a prophet?” He replied: “I am neither a prophet nor a prophet’s son. Rather, I have received this tradition: If my prayer flows readily in my mouth, I know it has been accepted; otherwise, I know it has been rejected.” They sat, wrote down the time, and noted it precisely. When they returned to Rabban Gamliel, he said: “By the Temple service! You have neither subtracted nor added. At that exact time the fever left him, and he asked us for water to drink.”’

paragraphs.text: Nedarim 20b: After Rabbi Levi states that a woman who explicitly demands intercourse from her husband is called brazen and has morally defective children, the Gemara asks: ‘But Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in Rabbi Yonassan’s name: A man whose wife solicits him has children whose like did not exist even in Moses’ generation. It is written: “Provide yourselves with wise and understanding men,” yet “I took the heads of your tribes” does not mention understanding. It is also written: “Issachar is a strong-boned donkey,” and “Of the descendants of Issachar, who understood the times.”’ This concerns a woman who wins her husband’s favor and entices him, rather than explicitly demanding relations.

paragraphs.text: Introduction to the Zohar 2a, Sulam translation: ‘Within the concealed holy lamp—Malchus included within Binah—He engraved a concealed image, the Holy of Holies: a deep structure emerging from thought, the mystery of the three upper sefiros. It is called Mi, “Who,” the beginning of the structure. It stands and does not stand, deep and hidden within the name Elokim, and is still called only the Mi of Elokim, since the letters Eleh, “these,” are absent from that name. It wished to reveal itself and be called Elokim, so it clothed itself in a precious, luminous garment, the light of kindnesses. It created Eleh, and the letters Eleh entered the name Elokim. These letters joined those—the letters Mi joined Eleh—and the name Elokim was completed. Until it created Eleh, it did not attain the name Elokim. Those who sinned with the calf said of this mystery: “Eleh—these are your gods, Israel.”’

paragraphs.text: Kesubos 110b: The Sages taught: "A person should always live in the Land of Israel, even in a city whose inhabitants are mostly gentiles, and should not live outside the Land, even in a city whose inhabitants are mostly Jews. Whoever lives in the Land of Israel resembles one who has a God; whoever lives outside the Land resembles one who has no God, as it is said: 'To give you the land of Canaan, to be your God.'" Does everyone who does not live in the Land have no God? Rather, it comes to tell you that whoever lives outside the Land is as though he worships idols. Likewise, concerning David it says: "For they have driven me away today from sharing in the Lord's inheritance, saying: Go, serve other gods." Did anyone actually tell David, "Go, serve other gods"? Rather, it comes to tell you that whoever lives outside the Land is as though he worships idols.
